Amazon , Uber , and Instacart have sued New York City to block a law that limits when app-based delivery companies can remove workers from their platforms. The lawsuit, filed Oct. 28 in Manhattan federal court, challenges rules scheduled to take effect Jan. 17, 2027.
What’s Related
The companies argue that the law violates their constitutional rights to free speech and due process. They plan to seek a preliminary court order preventing enforcement while the case proceeds, Reuters reported.
Known as Local Law 34, the measure generally bars companies from permanently removing delivery workers after a 30-day probation period without a work-related reason, a legitimate economic reason, or a legal requirement. Deactivation means a worker loses access to the app or permission to accept deliveries.
The law also lets workers challenge certain deactivations from the six years before it takes effect. That provision could require companies to revisit decisions dating to 2021.
RELATED STORIES: New York City’s Delivery Boom Is Leading to More Crashes and Injuries | Amazon Delivery Vehicles Got Over 14,000 Citations in NYC, Analysis Finds
What the law requires
For misconduct or poor performance, companies generally must use a series of disciplinary steps, such as warnings or additional training, before deactivating a worker. The law makes an exception for egregious misconduct, which can include violence, theft or sexual harassment, depending on the circumstances.
Companies must give written notice with detailed reasons within 72 hours of any deactivation. For layoffs based on economic reasons, they must also give 120 days’ advance notice. For layoffs based on economic reasons, they must give 120 days’ advance notice.
Workers can challenge a removal through an informal process with the company or ask the city’s Department of Consumer and Worker Protection to investigate. Workers wrongfully deactivated after the law takes effect could receive lost earnings and reinstatement.
Instacart raises safety concerns
In an Oct. 28 statement, Instacart said the rules could make it harder to remove accounts over safety concerns or fraud. It also argued that reopening older cases could restore access to people previously removed for those reasons.
The company said required disclosures could expose sensitive customer information or reveal how it detects fraud. Instacart also acknowledged the consequences for workers who lose access to delivery jobs .
“Losing access to the platform without a clear explanation can be upsetting, and we hear that feedback,” the company said.
Earlier removals face review
The law does not automatically restore every previously deactivated account. It allows workers to petition for reinstatement and generally requires companies to restore access within 30 days unless the earlier removal meets one of the law’s exceptions.
Instacart said its current process already gives shoppers a specific reason for deactivation and an opportunity to appeal. It also said a human reviews final deactivation decisions.

Schneider will make Norfolk Southern its primary eastern rail provider under an agreement announced Oct. 29 aimed at expanding domestic intermodal capacity and giving shippers more options to move freight across the eastern United States.
The agreement, effective in November, shifts Schneider’s NYSE: SNDR ) company-owned equipment, drivers and logistics operations away from CSX (NASDAQ: CSX ) and pairs it with Norfolk Southern ’s 22-state intermodal network. The companies said the partnership would expand market access, increase capacity flexibility and help attract freight now moving by truck.
“As we transition our primary eastern rail provider to Norfolk Southern, we’ll expand access to key markets, increase network flexibility and create new opportunities to better serve our customers,” said Michael Baumgardt, Schneider’s executive vice president of intermodal and logistics, in a release.
The move comes as NS pursues a transcontinental merger with Union Pacific (NYSE: UNP ).
Schneider’s intermodal operation includes approximately 23,900 chassis, 26,800 containers and more than 60 rail hubs across North America. Its company drivers handle more than 90% of its domestic dray moves, the companies said.
Norfolk Southern (NYSE: NSC ) said the partnership builds on a series of infrastructure and service investments intended to accommodate customer growth. Those projects include new service between Cincinnati and Atlanta, double-stack clearance improvements linking the Midwest and New England through its East Edge route, and terminal expansions in Ohio, Michigan, North Carolina and Illinois.
The railroad is also upgrading pavement, lighting, storage areas, maintenance facilities, truck access and security at terminals in several markets, including Atlanta, Louisville, Harrisburg, Chicago and St. Louis. Norfolk Southern said the work is intended to improve reliability and reduce the time drivers spend moving through terminals.
“Customers are taking a broader view of intermodal than ever before, and we are investing ahead of that demand,” said Ed Elkins, Norfolk Southern’s executive vice president and chief commercial officer.
Norfolk Southern reported that its intermodal volumes grew 3% in the third quarter of 2026, citing steady consumer demand, favorable truck-market conditions and network improvements. The companies said the new agreement would support further growth by broadening Schneider’s reach and creating opportunities to convert truckload shipments to intermodal service.
The announcement did not disclose financial terms, quantify the additional capacity expected from the partnership or specify a transition date.
Why it matters: While a key win for NS, a longer-term connection to the proposed Union Pacific–Norfolk Southern merger gives Schneider access to additional intermodal markets by reducing the difficulties associated with shorter rail hauls and transfers between railroads.

Alnylam shares dropped by a quarter on Thursday, with analysts suggesting the decline puts the RNAi specialist within range for a takeout.
Alnylam managed a 59% increase in revenue for its transthyretin franchise in the third quarter but a convergence of uncertainties has sent the big biotech “back to the penalty box,” according to analysts.
The franchise, which includes Amvuttra and Onpattro, collected $1.15 billion for the period , a major increase over the same period a year earlier. But the remaining quarter will be a tough slog for Alnylam, with pressures on inventory and pricing.
“While we remain positive on the TTR franchise and Alnylam’s long-term prospects overall, the trifecta of uncertainties is placing significant pressure on the stock,” BMO Capital Markets wrote on Friday morning.
Alnylam’s shares fell by a quarter at market close to $174. The stock is down 56% year to date. Alnylam currently has a market cap of $23.3 billion.

Oppenheimer said the plummeting stock has grown the case for a potential takeover of Alnylam, with Sanofi the most likely buyer.
On a Thursday earnings call, CEO Yvonne Greenstreet admitted that, despite a large effort to build out Amvuttra, the uptake has not been what the company had hoped.
“Look, we’re not satisfied with the pace of our future demand growth, and we need to do better,” Greenstreet said. “That being said, we have delivered substantial growth since the launch. It’s early days, and we think we’ve got significant opportunity ahead of us, and we’ve built a very strong foundation. And all the market fundamentals remain favorable.”
Greenstreet professed confidence in the clinical profile of Amvuttra in transthyretin amyloid cardiomyopathy (ATTR-CM), pointing to clinical evidence that the TTR silencer has shown a reduction in death and cardiovascular events.
Amvuttra was initially approved by the FDA in 2022 for ATTR with polyneuropathy (ATTR-PN). The drug was cleared for ATTR-CM in March 2025. The second launch has not been smooth, with Alnylam forced to cut guidance earlier this year as sales for the drug fell short of analyst expectations. Pressure is building on the franchise as competitors from BridgeBio Pharma and Pfizer steal market share.
Also putting pressure on Alnlyam is the upcoming 340B drug pricing rule update, which will impact the pool of money available for certain drugs—Amvuttra included—offered through Medicare.
“While the proposed rule would not become effective until January 1, 2027, our interactions with health systems over the last few months suggests that it could create Q4 ordering volatility as providers assess the implications for their economics and site of care choices,” CFO Jeffrey Poulton explained.

Alynlam has declined to say how much of its Amvuttra volume will be impacted by the 340B changes, but Truist Securities estimates that about 15-20% could be “directly exposed,” according to a Thursday note.
Greenstreet insists that the physicians who give Amvuttra a try prefer it with their patients. Alnylam has therefore been targeting the two-thirds of potential prescribers who have yet to write a script.
“What we need to do is build familiarity to drive adoption,” she said. “We’re very confident that we’ve made the right investments, and this is the right strategy, and we’re focused on driving execution with urgency.”
Meanwhile, Greenstreet warned analysts not to expect growth for the fourth quarter as that work continues. Alnylam reiterated its guidance on Thursday, with expectations of net product revenue between $4.7-$5.1 billion, with the TTR franchise landing between $4.2-$4.5 billion. Poulton said revenue for the full year will likely fall on the low end of that scale.
Investors will have to wait for 2027 guidance, too. While Alnylam traditionally releases its next year expectations prior to the J.P. Morgan Healthcare Conference, which takes place mid-January every year, analysts noted that executives have pushed that out to February 2027.
“We view the departure from historical guidance timing as another indication of heightened uncertainty entering 2027,” Truist wrote.

First Owner Got No-Markup Plymouth Superbird, Picked It Up After 6 Months, It's an Amazing Survivor
31 photos
Photo: YouTube/Mopars5150
Rain-soaked timber country rarely advertises its greatest mechanical treasures, and the quiet logging town of Vernonia, Oregon is no exception. Behind the weathered brick facade of the former Vernonia Auto Company—a historic dealership that first opened its doors to sell new 1938 Chevrolets—restorer and lifelong collector Gary Myers presides over a subterranean labyrinth of Detroit iron that will leave you speechless.
Stepping past an original 1938 porcelain neon dealership sign is like crossing the threshold into an untouched muscle car sanctuary. Parked nose-to-tail across two crowded levels sit two 1970 Plymouth Superbirds, a 19,000-mile (30,578-kilometer) 1969 Plymouth Hemi Road Runner coupe, a 1-of-36 1968 Plymouth Hemi GTX convertible, a California black-plate 1968 Dodge Hemi Charger, and a genuine 1970 Plymouth Road Runner 440 Six-Barrel bought for a single $100 bill.
The roster stretches even further into the shadows of the workshop. A Spring Green 1969 Dodge Charger R/T reunited with its factory drivetrain shares floor space with a triple-color 1969 Road Runner convertible, a heavily documented 1970 Road Runner 383 in Limelight green, an unrestored 1971 Chevrolet Camaro Z28 bearing a 1970s bullet hole, a 1962 Chevrolet Impala, a record-breaking Road Runner circle-track racer, and a dozen customer Mopars.
Yet every visitor's gaze inevitably locks onto the brightest jewel parked on the upper floor beside that glowing powder-blue Chevrolet neon sign. It is Gary's unrestored, 40,000-mile (64,374-kilometer) 1970 Plymouth Road Runner Superbird, a factory pistol-grip 4-speed survivor that wears its original paint, original vinyl top, and original factory assembly scars like badges of honor from the fiercest aerodynamic war in American stock car racing history.
Photo: YouTube/Mopars5150 To comprehend why such an outrageous machine ever rolled onto public streets, one must revisit the high-banked superspeedways of 1969. Chrysler Corporation was locked in a 200-mph aerodynamic battle against Ford Motor Company, and was losing. The Torino Talladega was mopping the floors with Mopar rivals, while then-triple champion Richard Petty had defected to Ford after Plymouth executives refused to build him a winged counterpart to the 1969 Dodge Charger Daytona.
Determined to win Petty back for 1970 – and the NASCAR wreath of laurels – Plymouth went to work, calling the missile engineers back for another round of wind-tunnel wizardry. While Dodge had satisfied 1969 racing rules by building just 503 Charger Daytonas—reportedly tricking inspectors by driving the same cars past counting officials twice—sanctioning officials raised the 1970 homologation mandate to one vehicle for every two franchised dealerships in the United States.
Offered for just a single model year in 1970, the Superbird required a minimum run of 1,920 cars, with Plymouth ultimately assembling a few extras, just to be on the safe side in case someone actually wanted to count each and every one of those. The most commonly accepted version is that there are 1,935 units, all assembled in late 1969. Quite a few are accounted for today - several of those have been rescued by Troy Bergeron, Mopars5150’s head car nut, who came to visit Gary and his collection.
Photo: YouTube/Mopars5150 Buyers in 1970 could select from three big-block engines: the 426-cubic-inch (7.0-liter) Hemi V8 rated at 425 hp (431 PS) and 490 lb-ft (664 Nm) of torque with 135 built, the 440-cubic-inch (7.2-liter) Six-Barrel V8 making 390 hp (395 PS) with 716 built, or the standard 440-cubic-inch (7.2-liter) Super Commando 4-barrel V8 producing 375 hp (380 PS) and 480 lb-ft (651 Nm) with 1,084 built, of which 4-speed manuals were 485.
Gary's 4-speed survivor hails from the third and final production batch, where workers at Detroit's Lynch Road plant and Clairpointe facility slammed the cars together to beat the December 31, 1969 deadline. As Gary demonstrates, the Superbird is literally a corporate half-breed: engineers grafted the 19-inch steel nose cone onto a Plymouth Road Runner body by bolting on modified front fenders and the hood from a 1970 Dodge Coronet.
Because this car has never been restored, every chaotic detail of that rushed 1969 assembly line remains preserved. Pitted air pockets and coarse grinder marks mar the factory lead filler around the nose cone, stray welding wires protrude from the hinges, factory paint runs drip down the door jambs, and inspector grease-pencil numerals—a 7 on one side and a 6 on the other—still grace the Dana 60 rear axle.
Photo: YouTube/Mopars5150 Despite its speedway pedigree, the towering 24-inch (610-millimeter) cast-aluminum rear wing repelled suburban buyers in 1970. A physician bought this car new at dealer cost on the condition that it remain on the showroom floor for six months to draw curious traffic. When he finally brought it home, his wife refused to ride in it unless the wing was removed, leaving minor scratches around the trunk mounting cutouts.
The doctor's son later drove the Superbird to college, clamping a ski rack directly onto the black vinyl roof pillars to haul snow skis up to Oregon mountain lodges. In June 1999, a friend sent Gary to Lowell, Oregon to inspect the car as a practical joke; the prank backfired when Gary bought the time capsule and later verified those exact ski-rack rub marks in a stunned phone call with the original owner's son.
Today, the car retains three original paper broadcast sheets—including one still tucked untouched beneath the center floor mat—alongside its original window sticker and ink-stamped spare tire. While Gary and his wife once drove it down Interstate 5 to Woodburn, dodging distracted motorists and 40-foot (12.2-meter) semi-trucks, this irreplicable piece of racing history now rests safely indoors, never to be sold during Gary's lifetime.

Acumen will implement cash-saving strategies and assess its options after sabirnetug failed to beat placebo, leaving the biotech without a clinical program.
Acumen Pharmaceuticals’ investigational amyloid therapy failed to improve cognitive and function in Alzheimer’s disease during a mid-stage study, prompting the company to discontinue development of the asset and seek strategic options.
The Alzheimer’s candidate was Acumen’s only pipeline program. Friday’s news sent the company’s stock plummeting 80% to 44 cents per share in pre-market trading.
The Massachusetts biotech was testing sabirnetug—also known as ACU193—in patients with early Alzheimer’s. The monoclonal antibody is designed to selectively target toxic soluble amyloid beta oligomers to address the hypothesis that they are an early underlying cause of the neurodegenerative process.
Topline data from Acumen’s Phase 2 ALTITUDE-AD study did not support that hypothesis, with no meaningful difference recorded between sabirnetug and placebo in cognitive and functional improvement at 18 months. Sabirnetug also failed to meet any key secondary endpoints.
The drug was generally well-tolerated, according to Acumen, though amyloid-related imaging abnormalities-edema (ARIA-E)—a treatment-related swelling of the brain— were observed in about 10% of sabirnetug-treated participants.
As such, Acumen has terminated clinical development of the asset, including an open-label extension of the ALTITUDE-AD trial. The biotech’s pipeline consists of sabirnetug in both intravenous and subcutaneous versions. The asset holds fast-track designation from the FDA for early Alzheimer’s.
“While we are disappointed the trial did not meet its primary endpoint, we express our compassion and hope for future therapeutic options for patients with Alzheimer’s disease and their families,” Acumen CEO Daniel O’Connell said in a Friday release. “We have tremendous gratitude toward the patients, caregivers, investigators and clinical trial sites, as well as all Acumen employees, who worked so diligently over many years on this program.”
The biotech now intends on implementing “cash conservation measures” and exploring strategic options. BioSpace has reached out to the biotech for more details on these measures.
One strategy the company is reviewing pertains to its enhanced brain delivery technology. In July 2025, Acumen teamed up with JCR Pharmaceuticals to combine its antibody science with the latter’s blood-brain barrier (BBB)-penetrating technology, J-Brain Cargo, in hopes of creating next-gen central nervous system therapeutics.
Better delivery to the brain has become a focus of the next wave of Alzheimer’s treatments, with companies like Roche and Eli Lilly exploring blood-brain barrier technology.

Waymo is adding the Toyota bZ4X to its robotaxi lineup. Toyota will build a custom version of the electric SUV with the Waymo Driver integrated right on the line in Japan, and a test fleet will start operating there in 2027.
It’s the first actual vehicle to come out of the partnership the two companies signed last year. And it gives Waymo a Japanese-built car for its Tokyo launch, with the UK and other markets to follow.
From “exploring” to building cars
When Waymo and Toyota first announced their deal in April 2025 , it was a preliminary agreement to “explore” working together on autonomous driving, including in personally owned vehicles. Lots of intent, no product.
Now there’s a product. According to Waymo’s announcement , Toyota will produce the vehicles at its Takaoka plant in Toyota City, Aichi Prefecture, and Waymo’s self-driving hardware will be installed and integrated at that same site instead of being retrofitted somewhere else.
Advertisement - scroll for more content
The robotaxi bZ4X gets a few rider-focused changes: extra rear legroom, automatic doors, a power liftgate, and ambient lighting. Waymo didn’t share sensor specs, unit volumes, or what each vehicle costs.
Operations in 2027 are about testing and validating the autonomous bZ4X fleet in Japan. The UK and “other Waymo markets” come in later years, with no dates attached.
The two companies also say they’ll keep working on autonomous tech for Toyota’s personal vehicles, plus safety projects with Woven by Toyota, the automaker’s software arm.
Waymo co-CEO Dmitri Dolgov said that “Toyota’s commitment to zero traffic accidents resonates deeply with us at Waymo.”
Waymo now has four vehicle platforms
The timing lines up with Waymo’s Japan plans. In September, Waymo said it’s targeting fully driverless commercial rides in Tokyo in 2027 with taxi operator Nihon Kotsu and ride-hailing app GO, scaling to about 100 vehicles, pending regulatory approval.
In the US, Waymo’s fleet is still mostly made up of Jaguar I-Pace SUVs, a model Jaguar no longer produces. It’s been adding the Zeekr-built Ojai van and the Hyundai Ioniq 5, and Hyundai is reportedly in talks to supply up to 50,000 Ioniq 5 robotaxis by 2028 .
The bZ4X makes four. It isn’t Toyota’s first robotaxi bZ4X either: Toyota and Pony.ai started mass-producing bZ4X-based robotaxis in China earlier this year.
For US readers, the refreshed model is sold here simply as the Toyota bZ, starting at $34,900. A cheap, high-volume base vehicle matters a lot when you’re trying to scale a fleet.
And Waymo is scaling. It now does over 500,000 paid rides a week across 15 US metros, and it picked Toronto as its first Canadian city earlier this month, with riders targeted for 2028.
Electrek’s Take
This is a big one, even if the bZ4X is about as exciting as a toaster.
Waymo’s biggest constraint right now is cars. It has been running a fleet built on a discontinued Jaguar, and every new automaker it signs adds manufacturing capacity it doesn’t have to build itself. Toyota is the world’s best-selling automaker. Having it build Waymo-ready vehicles on its own assembly line is exactly the kind of industrial partner Waymo needed.

Toyota and Waymo probably will follow through with offering the Waymo driver in personal vehicles, but it will probably take a while to get there, because of the need to map more roads. I believe it is simply a matter of time before it happens.

The 2027 Alliance Delta 252RL Is an Exceptional Travel Trailer for Couples Who Plan Long RV Trips
25 photos
Photo: Alliance RV
Nowadays, people don’t use their RVs only for short weekend escapes. Many spend weeks or months away from home, so having a well-equipped RV to call home on the road is an essential requirement. For couples looking for a travel trailer capable of supporting extended travel, remote work, or full-time RVing, the 2027 Alliance Delta 252RL is a phenomenal choice.
With residential living comfort, all-weather construction, a factory-installed solar package, Starlink prep, ample room for personal belongings, upgraded towing gear, and large waste capacity, this couples’ travel trailer is ready for extended boondocking stints.
Though it has only been around since 2019, Alliance RV is a well-known name in the RV industry. Founded by industry veterans Coley Brady and Ryan Brady, the company is one of the few independently owned RV manufacturers out there, and its goal is to deliver premium, lightweight RVs at an accessible price point.
But what helped it achieve notable success in a relatively short time is the company’s dedication to quality, innovation, and customer-driven product development. Instead of following industry trends, Alliance RV focuses on listening to customer feedback, and this helped it grow its lineup of RVs considerably.
Photo: Alliance RV The company’s Delta range of travel trailers, for instance, offers a slew of floor plans, so whether you’re a solo traveler, a couple, or a family that travels together, there is at least one model to suit you. The 2027 Delta 252RL presented here is a great example of the level of comfort and livability Alliance travel trailers are designed to offer.
Designed for couples who want to spend extended periods on the road in comfort and style, this model boasts a rear living layout (hence the “RL” in its name), with a private front bedroom and a walk-through bathroom, and offers a practical setup for longer trips .
It has an overall length of 29 feet 11 inches (9.1 meters) and a dry weight of approximately 6,545 pounds (2,968 kg), which makes it an agile half-ton towable. Equipped with dual axles, Goodyear Endurance tires, and a heavy-duty MORryde CRE3000 suspension system, the RV features an aluminum body construction with double-sided composite sidewalls, composite floors, and an all-new fiberglass front cap with an elevated logo.
Photo: Alliance RV On the campsite, an 8-foot (2.4-meter) power awning with dimmable lights, an exterior griddle/grill combo, and a stowable picnic table create the perfect setup for spending time outdoors. At the front, a large pass-through storage compartment provides space for large equipment and integrates the RV’s control center.
Two 20-pound propane tanks and a BAL auto-leveling system that makes setting up at a campsite easier are also included at the front, while an oversized rear ladder, a 300-pound rated accessory hitch, and a spray port are integrated at the back.
The Delta 252RL boasts a large slide-out and offers a rare two-door floor plan. The main door opens into the living area, while a private secondary door enters the front master suite, allowing access to the bedroom and bathroom even when the slideout is not deployed.
Couples who want a wide open floor space will love the interior of this travel trailer. The slideout, which houses a three-seat theater style sofa with atrium windows all around, considerably increases the living space. The theater recliners face a 40-inch Smart HDTV mounted on a swing arm, and an integrated electric fireplace adds warmth and charm.
Photo: Alliance RV A booth dinette is integrated at the rear of the trailer, providing a dedicated place to eat or work for two people. It comes with both under-bench and overhead storage and it also converts into a small guest bed. A dual pull-out pantry is neatly integrated next to the dinette, showing just how efficiently every square inch of space is put to good use.
The nearby kitchen has an L-shaped configuration, and though it’s not very large, it is well-equipped for cooking your own meals during extended adventures. It features solid-surface countertops with a flip-up extension, a matching backsplash, an oversized farmhouse-style stainless-steel sink, and a tip-out trash can, while the appliance package includes a three-burner cooktop, an oven, a microwave, and a 10 cu. ft. refrigerator.
The updated interior for the 2027 model year brings fresh cabinetry colors, new flooring, and slide fascia, as well as matte black cabinet hardware and residential-style cabinet doors. Soft-close hidden hinges and roller shades add to the residential feel and everyday practicality. Alliance RV has also kept the interior carpet-free, making it easier to keep the interior clean.
Photo: Alliance RV The private front bedroom has a residential feel and is separated from the main living area by the walk-through bathroom. It is fitted with a 60-by-80-inch (152-by-203-cm) walk-around queen bed, nightstands, wardrobes, under-bed storage, and device-charging ports built into the nightstands.
The bathroom is also designed for comfort on longer trips with a large 30-by-36-inch shower with a skylight, a porcelain foot-flush toilet, and an angled vanity with dedicated linen storage.
The travel trailer’s utility systems are also designed to support extended travel . The 252RL comes standard with a solar package that comprises a 200-watt solar panel, a 3,000-watt inverter, and a 30-amp MPPT solar charge controller. Other features that support the trailer’s touring capabilities include dual high-efficiency Furrion Chill Cube AC units, a Blu-Tech water filter, a tankless hot water heater, preparation for a backup camera, tire monitoring system, Starlink, and satellite equipment.
Photo: Alliance RV With a dry weight of 6,545 pounds (2,968 kg) and a gross vehicle weight of 8,550 pounds (3,878 kg), the Delta 252RL has a cargo carrying capacity of 2,005 pounds (909 kg). It carries 45 gallons (170 liters) of fresh water, 90 gallons (340 liters) of gray water, and 45 gallons (170 liters) of black water. The generous gray water capacity is useful for couples planning longer trips, allowing for more time between tank dumps. 12-volt holding tank heaters help protect the plumbing in colder weather.
All in all, the 2027 Alliance Delta 252RL travel trailer offers residential-style comfort and exceptional utility for long-term travel without entering the highest price brackets. Its MSRP starts at a reasonable $60,053.

While Mexican truckers have suspended a nationwide strike that disrupted highways across 19 states, industry leaders warned that demonstrations could resume if federal and state authorities fail to address grievances that include cargo theft and violence against drivers .
The suspension follows negotiations between Mexico’s Interior Ministry (Segob) and four trucking organizations — the National Chamber of Freight Transport (CANACAR), the Honorable Mexican Alliance of Transport Organizations (HAMOTAC), the Mexican-American Federation of Transporters (FEMATRAC) and the Organization for the Integration of Conventional Rights (INDECO).
The groups agreed to establish negotiations with multiple government agencies covering highway security, infrastructure, taxation, labor regulations and social security.
However, trucking leaders emphasized that the agreement represents a temporary suspension of protests rather than a resolution of the industry’s demands.
The demonstrations began Monday when truckers staged protests and highway blockades over cargo theft, extortion, violence against drivers and rising operating costs.
Mexico’s Interior Ministry reported demonstrations at 38 locations across 19 states, involving 691 vehicles and 858 participants. CANACAR disputed the government’s assessment, saying the protest movement extended across all 32 Mexican states.
Trucking leaders demand concrete solutions
At a Tuesday news conference following negotiations with federal officials, Carlos García Álvarez, national president of HAMOTAC, thanked truckers who participated in the demonstrations and credited their efforts with bringing government officials to the negotiating table.
The trucking organizations outlined agreements to establish working sessions with federal agencies responsible for public safety, transportation infrastructure, taxation and labor regulations.
Lauro Rincón Hernández, president of FEMATRAC, said highway security remains among the industry’s most pressing concerns.
“We cannot continue to endure more highway robberies, more loss of property, more truck drivers murdered,” Rincón Hernández said, according to Mexican transportation publication T21 .
Mexican trucking leaders pressed federal and state authorities during a news conference on Tuesday to create stronger measures against highway robberies, extortion and violence against commercial truck drivers. (Image: CANACAR)
The organizations are demanding stronger measures to prevent highway robberies, extortion and violence against commercial truck drivers.
According to various media reports here and here , CANACAR representatives said 15 truck drivers have been killed in Mexico this year, including three in Veracruz and two in San Luis Potosí.
Trucking representatives also expressed concerns that drivers and fleet owners are reluctant to report crimes because they fear retaliation from criminal organizations.
The industry has complained about difficulties recovering stolen commercial vehicles, even after authorities locate them.
García Álvarez told Mexican journalist Azucena Uresti that the demonstrations were suspended following months of discussions with federal officials, but highway insecurity remains unresolved.
“It seems like a crime to be a transport worker,” García Álvarez said.
Government agrees to four areas of negotiations
During the Tuesday news conference, the leaders of HAMOTAC, FEMATRAC, INDECO and CANACAR outlined four major areas of negotiations with federal officials.
The negotiations involve fiscal policies and fleet modernization about tax incentives, financing and measures to help carriers replace aging commercial vehicles; highway security, highway infrastructure, and labor regulations and social security.
Augusto Ramos Melo, president of CANACAR, said the trucking industry is seeking simplified social security requirements and more affordable options for small carriers and independent operators.
Ramos Melo said the discussions would also address proposed reductions in the workweek and how working hours and overtime should be calculated for truck drivers.
The CANACAR president emphasized that the industry is dominated by small businesses, making regulatory costs and administrative requirements particularly important.
He said the organizations would seek agreements with defined timelines rather than open-ended discussions.
Protests could resume if agreements fall short
Despite the suspension, trucking organizations have not ruled out renewed highway demonstrations.
Irma Serrano, FEMATRAC’s representative in Guanajuato, told Mexican news outlet La Silla Rota that national leaders had informed regional representatives about the agreements reached with federal officials.
Serrano said the suspension is temporary and depends on whether authorities establish specific commitments and deadlines to resolve the industry’s concerns.
No date has been announced for additional demonstrations.
Why it matters: Persistent cargo theft, extortion and attacks on truck drivers threaten Mexico’s transportation industry and the reliability of North American supply chains.

Strong immunology and neuroscience sales fueled AbbVie’s latest quarterly beat as the pharma’s stock continues to hit all-time highs.
AbbVie beat third quarter sales and earnings expectations and raised its full-year profit outlook Friday, powered by its immunology blockbusters and growing neuroscience business. Meanwhile, CEO Rob Michael said the company has plenty of capacity for more acquisitions but signaled a preference for bolt-on transactions over another megadeal like AbbVie’s $63 billion Allergan buy in 2020.
Both Q3 sales and earnings per share (EPS) came in above consensus estimates, with sales hitting $17.4 billion and EPS clocking in at $3.82.
The results prompted the pharma to raise its full-year EPS guidance from a range of $13.76–13.96 to $13.95–$13.99.
“Another beat and raise quarter should keep the AbbVie train rolling,” Guggenheim analysts wrote Friday before the company’s earnings call. Most of AbbVie’s key franchises came in at or slightly above expectations, according to the analysts.
The quarter adds to AbbVie’s momentum on Wall Street, continuing the pharma’s trend of trading at an all-time high. As of mid-morning Friday, AbbVie was trading at $294 per share.
Unsurprisingly, AbbVie’s immunology franchise drove the beat, bringing in $9.17 billion—16% year-over-year growth and aligning with consensus estimates. Blockbuster Skyrizi has grew 23% year-over-year to $5.7 billion. The pharma raised its full-year guidance for Skyrizi for the third time this year, now projecting $21.8 billion in sales, AbbVie Chief Commercial Officer Jeffrey Stewart said on the Friday investor call.
Meanwhile, autoimmune blockbuster Rinvoq experienced 24% growth to rake in $2.7 billion in the third quarter, modestly beating estimates and more than offsetting Humira’s 31% year-over-year erosion, according to William Blair analysts.
The most notable beat, according to William Blair, was AbbVie’s neuroscience portfolio, which recorded 19% year-over-year growth at $3.4 billion in Q3 revenue.
“In neuroscience, we’re on track to deliver growth of 20% this year, which has made us the industry leader,” Michael said on Friday’s call.
The neuroscience beat was fueled in part by antipsychotic Vraylar, with global sales topping $1 billion, reflecting a 14% year-over-year increase. Other contributors included a 100% jump for Parkinson’s disease drug Vyalev, 38% growth for migraine prevention pill Qulipta and a 27% rise for migraine treatment Ubrelvy.

“Given that our existing products or pipeline give us a clear line of sight to strong, durable growth into the 2030s, we have ample financial capacity to pursue the deals we’re interested in,” he said on the call when asked about M&A strategy.
“Now, I would expect these to be more bolt-on additions versus a large transformational deal like Allergan, and that’s because our business already has good breadth,” the CEO explained. “For us, it’s really more about adding further depth to these areas to drive that long-term growth.”
While AbbVie has one of pharma’s highest net debt balances—around $60 billion—Leerink Partners believes the company has plenty of leverage to execute.

Gov. Brian Kemp and Georgia Ports Authority officials celebrated the grand opening of the $134 million Gainesville Inland Port on Thursday, marking a new connection between Northeast Georgia’s manufacturing economy and international markets through the Port of Savannah.
The ceremony followed the terminal’s operational opening on May 4. The facility provides direct Norfolk Southern (NYSE: NSC ) rail service between Gainesville and Savannah five days a week, giving regional businesses an alternative to the roughly 600-mile round trip by truck.
“Georgia’s ports are a major reason companies choose to invest and create jobs here, and the Gainesville Inland Port brings that advantage directly to Northeast Georgia,” Kemp said. “Connecting this region to the Port of Savannah with new supply chain options makes it easier for Georgia businesses to reach customers around the world and helps ease congestion on our highways.”
The inland terminal extends Savannah’s port services into a region with more than 330 manufacturers, including poultry, heavy equipment and forest products businesses. Its rail connection gives shippers access to Savannah’s network of approximately 40 weekly vessel calls.
“With the start of operations in Gainesville, we’re extending the reach of the Port of Savannah deep into Northeast Georgia,” Georgia Ports President and Chief Executive Griff Lynch said when operations began. “Manufacturers across the region now have a seamless rail connection to more than 40 weekly vessel calls linking to global markets.”
Georgia Ports expects the terminal to shift 26,000 containers to rail during its first year of operation, reducing truck traffic and emissions on highways across Georgia, including in the Atlanta region. The agency has not disclosed volume at Gainesville since it opened.
Gainesville is the latest inland hub serving a major East Coast port. Georgia Ports also operates the Appalachian Regional Port serving Savannah, while South Carolina’s inland ports at Greer and Dillon handle boxes from the Port of Charleston. Virginia Inland Port at Front Royal, and North Carolina’s Charlotte Inland Port, alsop connect inland cargo markets to U.S. East Coast seaports by rail, although their terminal arrangements differ.
The 104-acre facility, formerly known as the Blue Ridge Connector, is designed to handle 200,000 containers annually at full build-out. It also offers access to Interstates 85 and 985.
Georgia Ports also funded $4.8 million in surrounding road improvements, including rerouting an access road, eliminating an at-grade rail crossing and resurfacing another road.
The opening comes amid industrial growth in Gainesville-Hall County. Since 2020, 78 new and expanding businesses have added more than 4,800 jobs and $2 billion in capital investment, according to figures cited by Georgia Ports. Manufacturing, processing and logistics account for 33% of the area’s workforce.
The Gainesville terminal is part of Georgia Ports’ nearly $5 billion, 10-year expansion program, which also includes additional cargo berths in Savannah and Brunswick.
Why it matters: The Gainesville Inland Port gives Northeast Georgia manufacturers a rail alternative to trucking goods to Savannah, a connection state officials say will lower freight costs, support industrial growth and reduce highway traffic.

CargoWise users handling British and Japanese customs declarations suffered messaging delays on Wednesday, while the backlog had been fully cleared the following morning.
Customer notifications seen by The Loadstar show WiseTech acknowledged an issue affecting message responses at 10.37am on 28 October. At 11.24, it confirmed that GB and Japan customs messaging were “particularly impacted”.
One UK forwarder said the disruption prevented its team from processing customs entries normally for much of the working day, leaving customers waiting and staff struggling to provide useful information.
The forwarder said its biggest concern was the impact on customers, that were “waiting and complaining”, adding “while operationally, we had very little we could tell them about when normal service would resume”.
WiseTech’s initial notification said its senior eServices team was investigating backlogs. Subsequent updates at 12.04 and 14.07pm said engineers were working on mitigation, before a 3.51pm notice reported backlogs ‘processing slowly’.
Customers were instructed not to resubmit messages awaiting replies, as this would worsen the backlog and could cause confusing rejections once both messages were delivered.
The forwarder criticised the support and escalation process, saying its team had followed the established reporting route, but received little actionable information as customer complaints mounted.
“My concern isn’t that a system outage happened, as clearly there will be occasions outside our control. It’s whether we have a strong enough escalation and communication process when it does happen,” the source said.
WiseTech’s notices show recovery work continued into the evening. At 8.47pm, the company said the backlog across most queues had been processed, but teams remained ‘engaged on the core issue’ and working towards full restoration.
At 8.33am yesterday, it confirmed that the backlog had been fully processed, and messaging services had recovered. However, it added that teams would continue monitoring while addressing the underlying issue.
The notifications span almost 22 hours, between acknowledgement and recovery confirmation, although they do not establish how long individual customers had been affected. The number of users impacted and the root cause remain unclear. The Loadstar has asked WiseTech Global to comment.
The disruption follows a separate CargoWise outage reported by The Loadstar in June, when customers in several countries experienced log-in failures and electronic messaging problems. WiseTech subsequently attributed that incident to a faulty data update.

Every carrier with a safety technology program eventually learns the same lesson: the hardware is the easy part. Cameras can be mounted, collision mitigation can be specified on new tractors, and telematics can be switched on. What’s harder to install is the belief, among people who spend their working lives behind the wheel, that the technology is on their side.
That gap between deployment and acceptance is where many programs succeed or stall. A fleet can invest heavily in sensors and software and still see limited results if drivers view the tools as surveillance instead of support. Carriers that close the gap tend to treat technology as one piece of a larger system that includes training, fair coaching and clear accountability.
Werner has spent years building that kind of system. Ryan Gass, Vice President of Safety and Terminal Management at Werner, walked through how the carrier approaches its safety program, from equipment decisions to driver trust to the role artificial intelligence is beginning to play in coaching.
A philosophy before a technology stack
For a carrier with a reputation as a safety leader among truckload fleets, the starting point isn’t a product. It’s a principle.
“Safety is one of our core values. It starts with the foundational belief that nothing we do is worth getting hurt or hurting others,” Gass said. That belief shapes how Werner approaches the tools it puts in front of drivers and safety staff.
According to Gass, the company relies on a combination of technology, training and accountability, with the goal of giving associates the tools to work proactively and giving drivers the best possible in-cab experience.
The order matters. Technology is positioned as a means of delivering on a value the company already holds, not as a substitute for it. That framing has practical consequences. When a fleet’s safety program starts with a commitment, every technology decision gets tested against a simple question: does this help keep people from getting hurt?
Newer equipment, more tools
One of the more direct ways Werner delivers on that commitment is through the equipment itself. Fleet age is often discussed in terms of maintenance cost and uptime, but it also determines which safety systems are available to drivers.
“We made a commitment to provide our drivers with a best in class experience with their equipment and that is reflected by the low average age of our tractors and trailers,” Gass said.
A younger fleet means the latest collision mitigation technology is more widely deployed across the company’s tractors. Werner is also in the process of outfitting its tractors with sideview cameras, adding to the forward-facing camera technology it adopted several years ago.
That layering reflects a broader pattern in fleet safety. Individual systems each address a specific risk, such as a following-distance event, a lane change or a backing maneuver. Combined, they give a carrier more complete visibility into what is happening around the truck and inside the cab.
What changes for the driver
For a driver, the question about any new system is practical: what does it change on the road?
Gass described collision mitigation as a “belt and suspenders” approach, an added layer of protection on top of the skills and judgment drivers already bring to the job. “Collision mitigation technology provides a belt and suspenders approach to our drivers adding in a layer of safety for our drivers,” he said.
There is in-cab coaching that provides active feedback and coaching to the driver. The sideview cameras also feed a monitor the driver can watch, which helps with blind spot monitoring during lane changes and while backing.
Those are everyday moments, and they’re where many incidents start. Giving drivers real-time information in the moment shortens the distance between a risky behavior and a correction.
Werner reports results on both sides of the ledger that safety leaders watch most closely. “We have seen a reduction in our accident/incident frequency as well as the severity,” Gass said.
The same data also serves the back office. Real-time information captured in the cab is available as evidence to assist with claim resolution, which turns a safety tool into a claims tool as well.
Trust is the real installation
Cameras raise a fair question for any driver: what happens to the footage? Gass was direct that the answer determines whether a program works. “Driver trust is extremely important to the success of any safety technology program,” he said.
Werner acknowledges drivers may initially have concerns about cameras and how the information collected will be used. Gass called those concerns understandable and said the company takes them seriously. The carrier’s response is to be explicit about intent.
“At Werner, our focus is on using technology to improve safety, not to micromanage our drivers,” Gass said.
In practice, that means transparency, consistent coaching and helping drivers understand how the systems can protect them. Video is a central part of that argument. When an incident occurs, footage can help establish what actually happened, which can protect a driver from a false accusation. Gass noted that driver acceptance improves when technology is used fairly and drivers see the benefits firsthand.
Privacy is part of the equation, too. Werner says it works to be thoughtful about what information it collects and how that information is used. Gass summed up the approach this way: “Ultimately, trust is earned through actions, not just policies.”
The goal, he said, is an environment where drivers see safety technology as a tool working for them rather than something working against them. For carriers weighing similar investments, the lesson is that rollout and communication deserve as much planning as the hardware.
Coaching at the scale of 8,500+ trucks
Technology generates data, but data only changes behavior when someone acts on it. At Werner, camera and telematics systems help identify behaviors so the company can address potential risks before they result in an accident.
The challenge is scale. “When you’re managing a fleet of 8,500+ trucks, delivering timely and consistent coaching across the organization is a significant undertaking,” Gass said.
Werner’s answer is to begin incorporating AI-generated coaching that uses the actual likenesses of its safety team. The idea is to deliver consistent, personalized coaching while keeping a familiar connection between drivers and the safety professionals they work with.
It’s a notable approach because it addresses a tension that many large fleets face. Personal relationships make coaching more effective, but personal relationships don’t scale easily. Gass sees AI as a way to resolve that tension rather than deepen it. “AI provides an opportunity to expand our coaching capabilities without losing the personal relationships that are so important to a successful safety program,” he said.
The company is still early in that effort, which Gass described as beginning to incorporate AI coaching. But the direction is clear: use technology to extend the reach of the safety team, not to replace the people on it.
Recruiting, retention and the business case
In a tight driver market, carriers naturally ask whether safety technology helps or hurts hiring. Gass offered a measured answer. “Technology alone isn’t necessarily going to recruit or retain a driver. However, a company that demonstrates a genuine commitment to driver safety, provides fair coaching, and invests in tools that help drivers succeed certainly has an advantage.”
That distinction is useful for fleet leaders. The tools themselves aren’t the selling point. The commitment behind them is.
The same logic applies to the financial case. Werner views safety technology as an investment in its drivers, its equipment and the long-term performance of its business, and Gass said the return goes well beyond the initial cost of the equipment. The company evaluates improvements in driver behavior, accident frequency, accident severity, claims expenses and overall operational efficiency.
According to Gass, Werner has seen significant reductions in critical safety events, DOT accidents and accident-related costs through its operations. Those results reinforce the importance of pairing the right technology with consistent coaching and accountability.
He was careful not to overstate what technology can do. “The technology itself doesn’t prevent every accident, but when it’s used effectively, it can make a measurable difference,” Gass said.
Then there’s the math of severity. Preventing even a small number of serious accidents can have a substantial impact, Gass said, both financially and, more importantly, on the lives of drivers and the motoring public.
What comes next
Looking ahead, Werner will continue looking at ways to leverage artificial intelligence. Beyond virtual coaching, the company is exploring predictive analytics, enhanced driver communication, and tighter integration among its camera systems, telematics and driver platforms.
Gass expects those connections to pay off over time. As the technologies evolve, he believes there will be more opportunities to identify emerging risks and intervene before an accident occurs.
He also drew a line around what the company will and won’t pursue. “Our focus isn’t on adding technology simply because it’s available. It’s about finding solutions that genuinely improve driver safety and make our operations more efficient,” Gass said.
That discipline may be the most transferable idea from Werner’s approach. Fleets face a steady stream of new safety products, and the temptation to adopt tools for their own sake is real. Filtering every option through a practical test, whether it improves safety and efficiency for drivers and the business, keeps a technology program focused.
The takeaway for fleet leaders
Werner’s experience points to a few consistent themes. Start with a safety commitment the whole organization can repeat. Invest in equipment that gives drivers current tools. Be transparent about how video and data are used. Pair every system with coaching that drivers experience as fair. And treat the data as a starting point, not a finish line.
Gass framed the larger goal this way: “The future of safety technology isn’t just about collecting more data. It’s about turning that data into meaningful action that prevents accidents and keeps America’s roads safer.”
For carriers still deciding how to build or expand a safety technology program, that may be the most useful measure of success: not how much information the fleet collects, but how reliably it turns that information into action, and whether the drivers on the receiving end trust it enough to use it.

After Hours Is a Passion Project Camper Van With Soft Blue Cabinetry and Trail-Ready Capability
23 photos
Photo: YouTube Screenshot / Summit Vans Australia
Meet After Hours, a conversion based on a 2024 AWD Mercedes-Benz Sprinter with a 144" wheelbase. Why this name? Well, it was built by Shane from Summit Vans Australia as a personal project on his own time, after hours and during the weekends.
Summit Vans is a Wollongong, Australia-based company specializing in high-end camper van conversions. Shane was actually the first ever employee the two founders hired.
Since Shane worked on the van when he had spare time, it took him almost two years to complete the build. He designed it as a personal family adventure van. He had been using it for a couple of years. A few months ago, he listed it for sale, and it quickly made its way to the new owner shortly after.
You can definitely tell that this van was built by a professional. Before we take a more in-detail look at the interior, let's see what we can find on the outside.
The vehicle rides on Summit Vans wheels wrapped in all-terrain tires. Shane took things up a notch and, together with Summit Vans, they used this rig as a test mule for a new shock kit done in collaboration between Summit Vans and Bilstein Australia.
Photo: YouTube Screenshot / Summit Vans Australia Specifically, the van sports a Bilstein 5160 rear shock retuned to fit a Sprinter van, a GVM (Gross Vehicle Mass) upgraded rear leaf spring, Baja brackets, a front auxiliary shock, and a front Bilstein B60 strut replacement.
At the front, you'll come across a Weldbeat bull bar that continues into a skidplate underneath. On the opposite end, Shane fitted a spare tire carrier/ladder and a Flarespace snowboard rack.
Climb on top of the van, and you'll find a Wedgetail roof rack. It holds four front-facing Stedi light pods (two clear and two amber), a cargo box with an 80 W solar panel on top, Maxtrax traction boards, a Fiamma awning, a snowboard rack, and two 200 W solar panels. The roof also has cut-outs for two Maxxair vent fans.
Other notable mods include Weldbeat side steps, power and water hookups, and a set of flares. Flares, also known as pods or capsules, are designed to increase the van width to allow you to fit a bed inside in an east to west arrangement instead of the normal north to south.
Photo: YouTube Screenshot / Summit Vans Australia Stepping inside, you'll be greeted by a clean and functional interior. Regarding aesthetics, Shane opted for a slatted bamboo ceiling with recessed LED light strips, wall panels upholstered in grey woven vinyl fabric, soft blue laminated cabinetry, and grey woven vinyl flooring.
The interior has an open layout, with no wall separating the driver's cabin from the living space. In the top part of the cabin, you'll find a large headliner shelf with an L-Track that allows you to hang gear or set up a curtain to separate the two areas.
This open layout allowed for better use of the overall space. For instance, the front part of the interior was turned into a seating area. The driver and passenger seats are mounted on swivel bases, so they can be turned around to face the back of the van.
The seating area continues just a bit further back in the form of a double bench seat straight ahead as you enter.
Photo: YouTube Screenshot / Summit Vans Australia You'll notice a fold-down table in between the bench and the two cabin seats, attached to an L-Track integrated into the wall. Another L-Track higher up offers additional mounting points and holds a soft overhead cabinet.
Next, we have a kitchen on the passenger side, by the entrance. It features a deep black stainless steel sink with a cover, a 65-liter Bushman's fridge with a tiny freezer compartment, and a portable induction stove.
A pull-out pantry and two drawers are available for storage. There's also an overhead cabinet that hides the "command center" for the rig's utilities. It includes a variety of light switches, some of which are dimmer switches, as well as a battery monitor and a timer switch for the water heater.
Shane even found the space to devise one of the most sought-after facilities in camper vans: a bathroom. It sits opposite the kitchen and offers a shower with a handheld wand and a toilet. Moreover, a roll-down door prevents any water from splashing outside.
Photo: YouTube Screenshot / Summit Vans Australia The bathroom can also double as a drying room. It has a vent connected to a diesel heater that pumps hot air and a wall-mounted L-Track that you can use to hang your clothes and gear.
Your bulkiest items are meant to go on the largest storage area inside this van: the garage underneath the bedroom, which is accessible from both inside and outside the van.
The garage offers heaps of storage space in the middle, and makes accessing your items easier thanks to a pull-out tray. Furthermore, on the sides, there are two black hex-ply boxes that accommodate the utility systems.
Power is on the left side – the electrical heart is a Bluetti AC240P portable power station . It has a 2,400 W AC output and a 1,843 Wh capacity and stays topped up thanks to three charging sources: solar power, shore power, and DC-DC charging.
Photo: YouTube Screenshot / Summit Vans Australia On plumbing, the van is equipped with two water tanks (one for fresh water and the other for grey water), an outdoor shower connection, and a Dieselheat DH9 hydronic heater. The latter provides both heated air and hot water.
All in all, it's obvious that Shane put a ton of work into his After Hours build. Not only does it pack so many creature comforts and offers abundant storage space, but it also has a welcoming, home-like design.

V-Code Gem: 1970 Plymouth Superbird Is All-Original, Unrestored, and Numbers-Matching
11 photos
Photo: CARFINDER/YouTube
Unhappy with how the standard Charger and the improved Charger 500 fared on NASCAR ovals, Dodge created the radical Daytona in 1969 . Fitted with a long nose cone and a massive rear wing, it was unlike anything else available in dealerships. In 1970, Plymouth created its own version, the Superbird.
When the Daytona arrived, NASCAR homologation rules required that at least 500 units be produced for public consumption. Dodge built 503 examples, and they sold like hotcakes. In 1970, however, NASCAR raised the production requirement to one car for every two manufacturer's dealers in the United States. This rule forced Plymouth to build at least 1,920 Superbirds.
The company put together 1,935 units and struggled to sell them. Unsold Superbirds reportedly sat on dealer lots until as late as 1970, with some even converted to Road Runner specs simply because no one wanted them. As a result, the Superbird is more common than the Daytona on the classic car market. It's also more affordable when it comes to non-Hemi examples.
On the flip side, all-original, unrestored examples are hard to come by. And these cars tend to fetch big six-figure sums, usually changing hands for over a quarter-million bucks. The TorRed "winged warrior" you see here is one of those vehicles.
Speaking of powerplants, the Superbird was available with one of three V8 engines. Just like the Charger Daytona, it came standard with the four-barrel 440-cubic-inch (7.2-liter) RB, with the mighty 426-cubic-inch (7.0-liter) Hemi on the options list. But it also got a mid-range option that the Daytona didn't have.
I'm talking about the six-barrel version of the 440 V8. The mill was introduced in 1969 on the Super Bee and Road Runner (part of the A12 package) and became widely available on B-body Mopars in 1970. The mill was rated at 390 horsepower, 15 more than the four-barrel 440.
Of the 1,935 Superbirds made, 135 were equipped with the Hemi, while 716 got the six-barrel option. The remaining units were fitted with the standard powerplant. This unrestored Superbird has the 6-BBL setup , confirmed by the V in its VIN. The mill is paired with a four-speed manual transmission, which narrows the production number to just 308 examples.
While survivor cars come with all sorts of flaws, this Superbird is an exception. I'm not saying it's flawless; I'm sure some issues may pop up at a closer look. But it's as close as it gets to being perfect, and that's mighty impressive for a Mopar that rolled off the assembly line a whopping 56 years ago as of 2026.
And that's precisely why it fetched big bucks at Mecum's Dallas/Fort Worth 2026 auction, which is where it was sitting on display when the video below was recorded. The Superbird crossed the block for $368,500, a sum that also includes the buyer's premium.
This sticker places it among the five most expensive V-code Superbirds ever sold at public auction. It's also one of only four V-code examples that fetched over $350,000. The all-time record was set in 2023 by a numbers-matching, low-mileage survivor in Lemon Twist paint . It sold for $550,000.
That same year, a restored automatic Superbird fetched $401,500. Finally, the third most expensive V-code Superbird, a highly optioned example, traded for $375,000 in 2026. Hit the play button below to check out this gorgeous time capsule.

KYIV, Ukraine — Ukraine has completed its share of Freyja, the multinational antiballistic shield that Europe and Kyiv are racing to bring together, the country’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, said earlier this month, putting the onus on partner countries and their defense contractors to develop the interceptor’s remaining components fast enough to conduct initial tests by year’s end.
Fire Point, the Ukrainian company leading the project , is building the FP-7.X interceptor and its launcher while partners such as Norway’s Kongsberg and Germany’s Diehl Defence are responsible for developing parts that find, track and guide the missile to its target.
“Ukraine has done what it was supposed to do, and that is good news,” Zelenskyy told journalists Oct. 17. “As for what the partners are supposed to do, you know that there are ten participating countries, and they are in the process.”
The push comes as Ukraine runs short of costly Patriot interceptors and Russia fields faster weapons, including jet-powered Shahed drones, forcing Kyiv to spend scarce antiballistics on both drones and increasingly large missile barrages.
Russia has fired more than 100 ballistic missiles at Kyiv and the surrounding region in the past two weeks after launching nearly 3,500 jet-powered drones across Ukraine in September, Zelenskyy said , quoting air force figures .
The Coalition of the Willing Summit on July 13, 2026, Paris, France. (X)
Civilian casualties from January through September ran 59% higher than a year earlier, according to the U.N.
“People work on systems like this for decades. We want it very fast, because there is no time,” Zelenskyy said about the new antiballistic system.
Freyja is designed to end Kyiv’s dependence on the Patriot and provide Europe with its own antiballistic capability. However, now that Ukraine has delivered the system’s base elements, one of the program’s most demanding phases – fitting European sensors, seekers and fire-control systems to a Ukrainian interceptor – hinges on partners’ pace of development.
Fire Point had already begun “the most intense and also the most complicated stage” of final assembly with specially designed radars and seekers from other countries, capping an overall effort to “squeeze a [antiballistics development] program that usually takes 20 or 30 years into a matter of a couple of years,” chief executive Iryna Terekh said in August.
Ukrainian officials consider the Patriot their only reliable defense against ballistic missiles, but the U.S.-Israel war with Iran has drained an estimated two-thirds of America’s prewar PAC-3 interceptor stock.
The missiles are also expensive and slow to arrive. A PAC-3 interceptor costs roughly $3.8 million, takes years to deliver, and can get held up in licensing talks or delivery issues.
Fire Point unveiled Freyja in May to end that dependence, offering Kyiv and its allies an interceptor they can build and deploy independently.
Ukraine and nine European partners, including France, Germany and the United Kingdom, officially launched Freyja’s coalition in Paris on July 13.
“Europeans themselves will be able to decide how many systems Europe needs and where they should be deployed,” Zelenskyy said at the launch . Poland joined the cohort in September, and Canada is “ready to contribute its technologies,” Zelenskyy said after meeting Prime Minister Mark Carney Sept. 10, according to the presidential office .
Under a June agreement with Germany’s Hensoldt , Fire Point is the prime contractor and design authority, and Hensoldt supplies the radars, such as the TRML-4D, which the company says can track roughly 1,500 air targets.
A preliminary design shared by Fire Point co-founder Denys Shtilerman on X in May pairs the FP-7.X with a long-range radar from Sweden’s Saab, France’s Thales or Hensoldt, a fire-control radar from Denmark’s Weibel or Italy’s Leonardo, and a command center from Kongsberg, maker of the NASAMS systems Ukraine already uses.
The system would tie into Ukraine’s wider air-defense network over NATO’s Link 16 standard, connect its radars through the Asterix protocol and use a two-way data link to correct the interceptor’s course in flight, according to the slides.
European partners will supply that data link and the command center, Reuters reported in June. Most of the system’s components are designed to be interchangeable.
The system’s seeker remains the bottleneck, Terekh told The War Zone , adding that Fire Point is integrating Diehl’s infrared seeker and developing other options with two unnamed partners.
“If we look at everything but the seeker, our production is already ready, even for mass production,” she said. “Even the seeker manufacturers are doing this for the first time in such an integration.”
The first FP-7.X will use a blast-fragmentation warhead, closer to the older PAC-2 than the hit-to-kill PAC-3, and intercept at roughly 12 to 16 miles (20 to 25 kilometers) up, Terekh told Janes in July. A hit-to-kill version will follow.
Fire Point aims to produce at least 2,000 interceptors a year for under $1.2 million (€1 million) each, though Terekh said that price would come “probably not from the first iterations, but definitely in serial production.”
Frejya’s next technical milestones depend on European partners.
“If, for example, every European government starts moving swiftly, we can do interceptors by the end of this year,” Fire Point’s Shtilerman said. The company is aiming for battlefield use next July.
In Oslo last week, Zelenskyy, Norwegian Defense Minister Tore Sandvik and Kongsberg chief executive Eirik Lie identified where work “can and must be accelerated to begin testing by the end of this year,” Ukraine’s presidential office reported.
“Fortunately for Europe and for Ukraine itself, we have Fire Point,” EU Defense and Space Commissioner Andrius Kubilius said Oct. 17, according to UNN , adding that its work on ballistic missiles and Freyja “could become a huge change.”

Jett McCandless, founder and CEO of project44 and LSP44, received the FreightTech Vanguard Award at FreightWaves’ F3: Future of Freight Festival dinner Monday, recognizing his contributions to the freight and logistics industry.
FreightWaves presented the award during F3 in Chattanooga, Tennessee, an annual event focused on innovation and the future of freight. The event also featured the FreightTech 25 , an annual ranking of the 25 most influential freight technology companies selected from the broader FreightTech 100 , which was announced in late September.
While the FreightTech rankings recognize companies for their current influence, the Vanguard Award recognizes founders for their long-term impact. McCandless was independently selected by FreightWaves for the award.
“So many technologies and innovations are driven by the vision, the relentlessness, the grind of our founders,” FreightWaves CEO Craig Fuller said as he presented the award. “We thought that this particular founder represented the best example of all of those characteristics.”
For McCandless, receiving that award on the F3 stage meant a lot.
“To have that recognition from him (Fuller) has made for one of the most proud moments of my life,” McCandless said.
McCandless founded project44 in 2014 to provide real-time visibility into shipments and supply chains. The company connects shippers, carriers and logistics providers with shipment data to help businesses track freight and manage transportation operations.
In July, project44 split its operations into two businesses : project44, which focuses on enterprise shippers, and LSP44, which provides artificial intelligence agents and application programming interfaces to logistics service providers, including freight brokers, forwarders and third-party logistics companies.
Fuller said project44 “defined a category” and has since extended its platform beyond where it started. He said McCandless’ path is what the award is meant to honor.
“I know that what they have built is not what they initially envisioned,” Fuller said. “I think that’s ultimately what being a founder is all about: applying grit, dedication, innovation, at times humility, admitting that things you set out to do may not be relevant currently, that markets change.”
McCandless dedicated the award to the people who handle freight’s worst moments.
“I want to accept this award on behalf of everyone who’s picked up the phone at 2 a.m. because a load went sideways,” McCandless said. “I’ve been that person, and I know a lot of you here have been too.”
Over the past decade, project44 has built a network that McCandless said now covers 286,000 carriers in 194 countries and territories and handles more than 700 million synchronized events a day.
The company’s next chapter is focused on AI agents . Building an agent is now the easy part, what makes one useful is how well it understands the freight industry and the different needs of the businesses operating within it, McCandless noted.
“‘On time’ means something totally different for a retailer than it does for a port,” McCandless said. “An agent that doesn’t know that isn’t smart. It’s just confidently wrong.”
McCandless described a future in which the 2 a.m. call never happens because the system already knows what went wrong, what the reroute options are and which carriers are best suited to handle it.
McCandless closed with a message for other founders in the room.
“To every founder out there doing the hard work, the unglamorous work: keep going,” he said.

VW Group’s operating loss swelled to €5.9 billion ($6.5 billion) in the third quarter because of a write-down of its Porsche stake, weak sales in China, and lower profit margins on electric vehicles.

Aurora Innovation cut its 2026 revenue forecast to about $9 million on Wednesday, down from the $14 million to $16 million reported in its second-quarter results , after a six-week manufacturing delay. The company reported third-quarter revenue of $3 million and an operating loss of $257 million.
Over the past month, output at Roush, which upfits Aurora’s trucks in Livonia, Michigan, was held back by material shortages, component quality problems and issues found in end-of-line testing, CEO Chris Urmson said on the earnings call. Aurora now expects Roush to reach 20 trucks a week in early December and delivering 200 trucks by the end of February
“Instead of producing 20 trucks a week in October, we’re going to do that in December, it really has no impact on our ability to go and scale and deliver a thousand trucks next year,” Urmson told Bloomberg, which interviewed him about Aurora’s quarterly results .
Aurora re-sources parts for the Roush line
Some of the delay traced to complex components that arrived late or below Aurora’s quality bar. Maday said Aurora moved some of those parts, including wire harnesses, to “a more capable production supplier.” He said that in most cases the change was cost-neutral or could save money once reduced rework is counted, and that it would not materially affect gross margin .
Other problems are typical of any new line, where some parts don’t fit together perfectly at first. Aurora Driver kits from supplier Fabrinet are running ahead of truck builds, and Roush is adding a second shift, Maday said.
“I really do think that this is just a little bit of a pivot to the right in terms of when we can start hitting the run rate, but there is nothing that is really prohibiting us from hitting the run rate at this point,” Maday said.
Aurora said Roush can push past 20 trucks a week by expanding the line.
Cash use rises with the fleet
Third-quarter revenue rose to $3 million from $1 million a year earlier. The operating loss widened to $257 million from $222 million and included $54 million in stock-based compensation. Net loss was $234 million, or 12 cents a share, compared with $201 million, or 11 cents, a year earlier.
Aurora used about $170 million in operating cash during the quarter and spent $36 million on capital expenditures, which it said was within its quarterly average target.
Asked by a Morgan Stanley analyst on the call whether the fourth-quarter increase reflected a structurally higher expense base, Maday said the money goes to hardware kits, components and truck builds at Roush. Research and development spending will change little, he said, with some added general and administrative cost to support hundreds of trucks.
“The vast majority of the increase is planned, it has been expected, and it is all related to building up the fleet,” he said.
The bill for the fleet is arriving before the revenue.
Aurora ended September with just over $1 billion in cash and short-term investments, down from nearly $1.2 billion at the end of June. During the quarter, it sold 6 million shares through its at-the-market program for $41 million in net proceeds and used $23 million of that to cover taxes on vesting employee stock.
Maday said Aurora should reach positive cash flow in 2028 with more revenue and fewer assets on its books, via Insurance Journal / Bloomberg News .
MOUs now cover 1,000 trucks
Charger Logistics signed a nonbinding memorandum of understanding to own and operate 500 Aurora Driver-powered trucks under Aurora’s driver-as-a-service model, with deliveries expected in 2027 and 2028. With Hirschbach Motor Lines’ 500-truck MOU in April , Aurora’s announced MOUs now cover 1,000 trucks.
The Charger MOU builds on the transportation-as-a-service agreement Charger signed with Aurora in July for freight between Dallas and Laredo, Texas. Aurora said the deal represents a potential multiyear revenue stream in the hundreds of millions of dollars.
“Since launching autonomous operations along the Laredo corridor, we’ve realized immediate operational benefits that point to a clear path to scaling,” Charger President Andy Khera said in Aurora’s shareholder letter.
Maday said Aurora and its customers agreed on pricing and volumes in the MOUs and that the remaining terms are operational, such as who services the trucks and how they are disposed of at the end of their lives.
“On the two MOUs, we fully expect these to convert,” he said.
Urmson said the initial 200 trucks are fully contracted, and Maday said Aurora has 10 driverless customers.
Weigh stations, customer sites and beacons
Autonomous trucks have relied on voluntary enhanced pre-trip inspections, or EPTI, to bypass weigh stations, Aurora said in its shareholder letter. Its system can now determine whether a station is open, pull into an available scale lane and handle different scale layouts, the company said.
“EPTI is a really useful tool that allows you to have certainty and bypass weigh stations, but it also adds complexity in training and operations at customer sites,” Urmson said.
In November, Aurora trucks will begin running directly to sites for several driverless customers, including navigating security checkpoints on their own.
Federal rules require the driver of a stopped truck to set out reflective triangles or flares. On Oct. 7, the Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration granted a five-year exemption letting Level 4 autonomous trucks use cab-mounted amber beacons instead. Other carriers running Level 4 trucks can use it after notifying the agency, according to the Federal Register notice .
Volvo and PACCAR to follow Roush
Roush is the first step in a phased manufacturing plan. Aurora is integrating its driver directly on Volvo’s factory line while preparing for full production with Volvo and PACCAR, according to the earnings release. Volvo Autonomous Solutions plans to launch driverless trucks with the Aurora Driver in the first quarter of 2027 and deploy more than 300 that year. AUMOVIO plans to start production of Aurora’s third-generation hardware kit in the second half of 2027.
Urmson tied the end-of-2027 goal back to February.
“We still expect to get 200 trucks out of this in February, and we see this still enabling the 1,000+ trucks we expect on the road by the end of next year,” he said.
Why it matters: Aurora still needs more than 1,000 trucks on the road by the end of 2027, now from a later start. For Charger and Hirschbach, whose 1,000 trucks still need binding contracts, and for investors facing a $250 million quarter, December’s 20-truck week at Roush is the next test.
