5 of the Quirkiest Engines the Volkswagen Group Ever Produced at the Orders of Ferdinand Piech
31 photos
Photo: Volkswagen AG
There was a time, only a few decades ago, when the Volkswagen Group was not only in a much better place than it is currently heading, but was arguably on its highest roll to date.
Not exactly a coincidence, that era started in 1993, when Ferdinand Piech became Chairman of the Group and immediately started a revolution that completely transformed the company. What followed across the next 22 years was a period of automotive engineering shenanigans that have never been repeated in Wolfsburg, and they probably never will.
I say this because the context in which it happened was simply unique. Ferdinand Piech was a genius engineer in complete control of a company with almost unlimited resources, and shareholders quickly learned that it was more fruitful to let him make whatever he wanted instead of arguing with him.
The total trust in him didn’t come immediately, but following a short period in which Piech’s managerial and engineering decisions upgraded the VW Group from the brink of bankruptcy to an automotive giant in almost no time. In 1993, VW lost approximately $1.1 billion USD due to soaring production costs, a drop in European sales and an inefficient cost structure.
The company was facing severe financial strain and was considered on the brink of bankruptcy due to soaring production costs, a drop in European volume markets, and inefficient management. Becoming the head honcho during the crisis prompted Piech to launch a massive restructuring effort that returned the group to profitability by the following year.
With the financial status becoming secure, Ferdinand slowly started to show his true motives for running the VW Group, with the main one being his dream of transforming it into the number one car company on the planet. He stopped short of usurping Toyota and General Motors, but during his tenure he did transform VW from a regional European carmaker into a global multi-brand empire, adding a number of highly coveted luxury brands to its roster and creating some of the coolest cars in the process.
For his contributions, he was named “Car Executive of the Century” in 1999, and his job at VW was only half done. Among the many changes Piech made to the company, he also introduced a number of innovations in Wolfsburg, including pioneering a standardized modular platform strategy across the entire group, and accepting no compromises regarding product quality.
A trained engineer by trade, he also became known for putting a lot of resources into expensive vanity projects , like the luxurious Volkswagen Phaeton or the mind-boggling Bugatti Veyron, and also for introducing a number of quirky engines that only cars from the Volkswagen Group used. This engineering excess was seen in almost every brand of the empire he had created, including under the hoods of cars that didn’t really need it.
With that in mind, I decided to curate a list of some of the most eccentric powertrains that Piech was personally responsible for being created and used. Most of them were commercial disasters, but all of them were magnificent for one reason or another, and none of them should be forgotten.
Volkswagen Beetle RSI: The Limited-Edition V6 Hot-Hatch that Wasn’t a V6 Launched in 1998, the retro-looking New Beetle was heavily inspired by the original Volkswagen Beetle when it comes to its exterior, while its architecture was completely switched around. Thanks to it using the VW Golf Mk IV’s platform, it was FWD with a transverse engine in the front instead of RWD with the engine in the rear, like the original.
In short, it was designed to be charming and invoke an emotional association with the first Beetle, especially the ones sold in the 1960s during the “Flower Power” movement, which is why each one came with a tiny flower vase in the dashboard. The New Beetle wasn’t designed to be practical, or fast, for that matter, but more as a lifestyle vehicle. Its most powerful engine in the beginning was a naturally aspirated, 2.3-liter five-cylinder with 170 PS (168 HP) that was quirky in its own right by being a V5, or VR5 as VW called it.
Photo: Volkswagen AG Its place at the top of the food chain was taken by a 3.2-liter VR6, which powered no more than 250 units of the Beetle RSI, launched in 2001 as the coolest version of the New Beetle, by far. Some would say that its $100k+ price and its motorsport-inspired looks were its most important attributes, but there are plenty others who became completely infatuated with its now legendary engine.
Especially for 2001, the engineering under the hood was simply extraordinary. The RSi debuted the 3.2-liter VR6 with four valves per cylinder, a naturally aspirated V6 that had more things in common with an inline-six cylinder engine than a V-angled one. This was not the first narrow-angle V6 made by VW , but it was the first one to debut the upcoming 24-valve 3.2-liter family of such engines, some of which would even arrive under the hoods of Porsches, not to mention the glorious Golf R32.
From some perspectives, the limited-edition Beetle RSI was more of a test bed for the engine, and despite “only” delivering 224 PS (221 HP), it used many motorsport-derived features that made it unique, even compared to the more powerful versions that followed. It came from the factory with a massive carbon fiber intake airbox to optimize airflow and boost induction sounds, and had a dual-exit exhaust system tuned by Austrian manufacturer Remus. To squeeze the wider block and a Haldex-based AWD system into the tight Beetle engine bay, there was no room for air conditioning routing, and the car famously even relied on manual window cranks to save weight.
Volkswagen Passat W8: The Only Production W8 Engine Ever Built Powered a Family Sedan Like with the Beetle RSI and its V6 with a 15-degree angle, the question of why the Volkswagen Passat W8 existed in the first place has both a simple answer and a complicated one. Believe it or not, both those answers are related to Ferdinand Piech, and both need the appropriate context.
Coincidentally, it was also unveiled in 2001, alongside the mid-cycle facelift for the B5 generation Volkswagen Passat, and its engine had more than one thing in common with the VR6 in the Beetle RSI. To create the peculiar 4.0-liter W8, Piech instructed VW engineers to make use of the modular concept from the EA390 VR6 family.
Photo: Volkswagen AG This is how, instead of a traditional 90-degree V8, with four cylinders on each side, the W8 practically consisted of two 15-degree VR4 engine blocks mounted onto a single, shared crankshaft at a 72-degree angle. This unique packaging solution made it incredibly compact for an 8-cylinder, measuring just 420 mm (16.5 in) in length, which is why it had no problem being fitted longitudinally under the hood of the B5.5 Passat, which could normally only house inline-fours and V6s at the most.
Again resembling the Beetle RSI, the Passat W8 was never intended to be a volume seller, with Piech deciding to make it as a test bed for the modular “W” engine concept that was about to take over many other brands of the VW Group, including Bentley and Bugatti. From that perspective, it’s no wonder fans of the model consider it “half a Bugatti engine.”
Unfortunately, the compact design and tight packaging came with some disadvantages as well, not to mention that it wasn’t exactly a pillar of performance with 275 PS (271 HP) from its 4.0-liter displacement. Maintenance costs were extremely high, as fixing basic elements from the rear of the engine sometimes required completely pulling the engine out of the car. Roughly 11,000 units in both sedan and station wagon guise were ever built, and no other production car in history has ever used a W8.
Volkswagen Touareg W12: The World’s First Unibody Twelve-Cylinder SUV The Volkswagen Touareg, as you all know, was developed jointly with Porsche, sharing its platform with the Cayenne and later with the Audi Q7, with the Bentley Bentayga and the Lamborghini Urus being created on the same underpinnings as well. From the beginning, it followed an entirely different recipe compared to its platform brothers, and it wasn’t supposed to go overboard with its engine lineup’s power range.
But then, someone at Volkswagen, with most of the fingers pointing, again, at Prof. Dr. techn. h.c. Dipl.-Ing. Ferdinand Karl Piech, decided that the Volkswagen Touareg needed a twelve-cylinder engine. That engine was the same 6.0-liter W12 developed for the Phaeton, which had already debuted on the Audi A8 and the Bentley Continental Flying Spur.
Photo: Volkswagen AG The powertrain had first appeared in various forms on a series of mid-engine supercar concepts, starting as early as the Giugiaro-penned 1997 Volkswagen W12 Syncro and ending with the record-breaking 2001 Nardo prototype. The Touareg W12 was only the world’s second-ever production SUV to feature a twelve-cylinder engine after the Lamborghini LM002 from the 1980s, also known as the “Rambo Lambo.” Coincidentally, Lamborghini was already part of the VW umbrella when the Touareg W12 entered production.
Initially, the model was supposed to be a limited-edition model, with just 500 units planned to be produced, 330 of which dedicated to the Saudi Arabia market. Eventually, the Touareg W12 became a production model and the halo version of the first-generation Touareg lineup. Naturally aspirated, it used a similar engine architecture as the Passat W8, with VW engineers fusing two banks of the same VR6 that debuted on the Beetle RSI together, and this gave it a length so short that it fit longitudinally without issues under the Touareg’s hood.
The downright insane idea that such a car should even exist as a production model was all thanks to Piech’s dreams of excessive engineering, which dominated most of the VW products during his tenure. Like the Beetle RSI and the Passat W8, the twelve-cylinder Touareg was not a commercial success, but that didn’t stop Ferdinand Porsche’s grandson from pushing for its existence.
Volkswagen Touareg V10 TDI: The Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde of Diesel SUVs Part of Ferdinand Piech’s master plan of upgrading the Volkswagen brand from a maker of “people’s cars” to a more premium one that could even go head to head with BMW and Mercedes-Benz required both new cars, like the Phaeton and Touareg, but also new technologies for its powertrains. One such technology was the proprietary “Pumpe Düse” technology for its diesel engines, which VW wanted to market against the competing Common Rail injection system.
For that marketing to work, Piech had the extravagant idea to create a halo diesel engine using the Pumpe Duse system, and this is pretty much how the V10 TDI came into existence, with the Touareg and the Phaeton being the first cars to be powered by it. From an engineering standpoint, the engine was not designed from scratch, making use of the modular technology that had also been used on the Passat W8 or the Touareg W12.
Photo: Volkswagen AG In essence, the V10 TDI effectively consisted of two 2.5-liter, inline-5 TDI engines fused together at a 90-degree angle. Therefore, the 2.5-liter R5 TDI and the V10 TDI shared the same cylinder bores and piston strokes, cylinder spacing and connecting rods.
Because it was structurally designed as two merged engines, the resulting 5.0-liter V10 also came with a number of engineering quirks, one of the most important being that it functioned using two of everything, including two separate engine control units (ECUs), two individual throttle bodies, two fuel pumps, and two mass airflow sensors.
This peculiarity was made even more obvious when you plugged a diagnostic scanner to it and the powertrain registered itself as being two distinct inline-5 engines. The 313 PS (309 HP) and 750 Nm (553 lb-ft) of torque it developed in the beginning made it the most powerful diesel passenger car on the planet, and this obviously weighed more than the potential reliability and maintenance problems its specific architecture also came with.
Audi Q7 V12 TDI: The Most Monstruous Passenger Car Diesel Engine in History Even compared with the ultra-intricate architecture of the gasoline W12, the V12 TDI stands tall as one of the most extreme engines ever fitted to a production road car. It is also one of the most in-your-face expressions of Ferdinand Piech’s personal conviction that excessive engineering can trump every other powertrain philosophy.
Apart from that, the Austrian also wanted to prove that the Volkswagen Group’s TDI badge was the most powerful diesel technology on the planet, so, once again, it needed a halo model. Following Audi’s 24 Hours of Le Mans successes using the TDI badge, Piech simply decided that there isn’t anything better to celebrate those victories than the world’s first (and so far last) V12 diesel.
Photo: Audi AG Initially, the 5.9-liter V12 TDI was supposed to power a version of the first-generation Audi R8 as well, and there was even a concept car, but the 2008 financial crisis and possible common sense kept Piech from giving it the go-ahead. Instead, the only twelve-cylinder passenger car diesel ever made was only offered on the first-generation Audi Q7.
Leaving the proprietary Pumpe Duse technology behind, the VW Group had already started switching to Common Rail technology by that time, so it wasn’t simply a case of taking the V10 TDI and adding two more cylinders at each bank’s end. Instead, the 5.9-liter V12 was actually created fusing two 3.0-liter V6s longitudinally, thus doubling their length. From this perspective, it was a much larger (and heavier) twelve cylinder than the gasoline W12, so it’s a wonder it even fit under the hood of the Audi Q7.
To squeeze the massive diesel powertrain into the Q7, Audi’s engineers had to completely redesign the model's front end, front axle, and cooling systems. The SUV was hand-assembled on a separate production line and came standard with massive 420mm carbon-ceramic brakes just to keep its massive 2.6-ton weight in check. It was never used on another car since, and its development costs were probably never recovered, but that only goes hand in hand with most of Ferdinand Piech’s quirky engine ideas.

Match equipment to the real duty cycle
Smart fleet planning starts well before a vehicle hits the road. Fleets often grow over time to include units that are rarely used, highly specialized or poorly suited to current work. A duty cycle is how much and how often a vehicle works. The U.S. Department of Energy recommends reviewing each vehicle's duty cycle as part of a broader fleet review to identify these gaps.
A good review asks a few simple questions:
Use : What tasks does each unit perform, and how often?
Fit: Is it the right type, class and size for the job?
Condition: Is it still cost-effective to run, or does it spend too much time out of service?
Dan Parks
Sustainability and cost control begin with picking equipment that matches the fleet's actual duty cycle. An oversized engine can affect equipment balance and burn unnecessary fuel, while an undersized one strains under load and wears out sooner.
Wise fleet managers choose the right engine size to shape fuel use, productivity, durability, maintenance and downtime for years to come. That makes it one of the simplest ways for fleets to balance resilience , cost and sustainability from day one.
Cut idle time before adding new tech
Idling is one of the easiest losses to fix. Argonne National Laboratory estimates that idling long-haul trucks burn more than 1 billion gallons of fuel annually at required rest stops.
Less idling also supports resilience. The same DOE guidance links lower petroleum use to more flexibility during natural disasters and fuel supply disruptions.
A few practical steps can help:
Set clear idle rules: Give drivers simple guidance on when to shut down.
Use telematics data : Flag the units and routes with the most idle hours.
Add idle reduction equipment: Auxiliary battery packs and similar units can power heating and cooling without running the main engine.
Switch to drop-in fuels where supply allows
Lower-carbon fuel doesn't always mean new vehicles. Renewable diesel can run in existing engines without changes to vehicles, storage or fueling equipment. That's why it's often called drop-in fuel.
Oakland, California, offers a real-world example. The city began moving its diesel vehicles to renewable diesel in 2015 and now runs its entire diesel fleet on fuel made from waste cooking oil. Since the pilot began, the fleet has cut fine particle pollution by 33% and nitrogen oxides by 9%.
In the UK, Adur & Worthing Councils switched their waste and recycling trucks to hydrotreated vegetable oil (HVO) in July 2025. HVO is a renewable fuel made from waste materials. The councils say the switch has cut the service's carbon emissions by up to 90% .
Supply varies by region, though. Fleets should confirm steady local availability before switching fully, so a greener fuel doesn't become a new weak point.
How to measure progress
Tracking fuel use and emissions in one place shows which changes actually pay off. The EPA's SmartWay program gives carriers and shippers a common system to track and share this data.
The results add up. U.S. trucking companies using the program have saved $55.4 billion on fuel bills to date. SmartWay also serves as a model for green freight programs in other regions, which makes it a useful reference for global supply chains.
Build a fleet that holds up under pressure
Balancing resilience, cost and sustainability isn't about finding a perfect trade-off. It's about choosing moves that serve multiple goals. Right-sized equipment and less idling cut spending and emissions while making operations steadier. Fleets that start there build a stronger base for bigger changes later.
Dan Parks is a senior writer at Modded.com with six years of experience specializing in supply chain content.

Posted By: Colin McClelland October 30, 2026
Stocks of uranium companies are falling despite the strongest long-term fuel prices in more than 18 years, as investors weigh an expected tightening of supply against rising costs and the difficulty of bringing new projects into production.
The VettaFi Global Uranium Mining Index, a benchmark tracking uranium mining shares worldwide, dropped 16% in September and the Nasdaq Sprott Junior Uranium Miners Index lost 22%, while spot uranium prices barely moved. Financial-market pressures appear to be overwhelming an improving fuel-market outlook, Sprott market strategist Paul Wong wrote in an Oct. 28 analysis .
“Even if the expected uranium price is unchanged, tighter liquidity can raise the cost of capital, compress valuation multiples and delay the market’s recognition of future project value,” Wong wrote. “Those effects are real, but they are cyclical and financial.”
The divergence matters because stronger fuel prices alone cannot deliver new production: developers still need permits, financing and years of construction. Sprott manages the world’s largest physical uranium fund, Sprott Physical Uranium Trust (TSX: U.UN; U.U), which held $7.6 billion (C$10.6 billion) in net assets as of Thursday.
Spot prices
Spot uranium prices are forecast to average $95 per lb. next year, up from an expected $88 this year, analysts at Fitch Solutions’ BMI wrote in an Oct. 15 outlook. Potential constraints on Kazakhstan’s production and increased utility purchasing underpin that forecast.
However, the near-term market is better supplied than the longer-term outlook might suggest. Global mine output is forecast to rise 7.8% this year, leaving a modest surplus when secondary supplies and demand from stockpiling and financial buying are included, BMI said.
BMI expects the market to shift into deficit next year. Its forecast suggests that expectations of future scarcity, rather than an immediate shortage, are supporting higher long-term prices.
Contracting strengthens
TradeTech’s long-term uranium price indicator held at $97 per lb. from June through September, up $13 from a year earlier and at its highest level in more than 18 years, the Colorado-based uranium pricing and nuclear fuel consultancy said in an Oct. 2 statement .
Utilities were seeking deliveries beginning as early as 2027 and extending into the late 2030s, TradeTech president Treva Klingbiel said.
An increase in natural uranium purchasing is likely in 2027–28 after utilities focused on securing enrichment and conversion services during the current contracting cycle, BMI said. Longer term, reactor uranium requirements are forecast to grow by an average 4.1% annually over 2026–35, ahead of mine production growth of 3.3%, BMI forecasts.
China’s reactor construction is the main demand driver. Some proposed Western projects are unlikely to proceed because of financing and regulatory barriers, BMI cautioned.
Kazakhstan presents a nearer-term supply risk. Commissioning of Kazatomprom’s (LSE: KAP) sulphuric acid plant has been delayed until between the third quarter of 2027 and the first quarter of 2028 after palaeontological specimens were discovered at the construction site, BMI said. The acid is essential to the country’s dominant method of uranium extraction.
Kazatomprom has said it does not expect the plant delay to materially affect mining operations, BMI noted. Nevertheless, the consultancy forecasts lower Kazakh output next year, reflecting its assessment of acid availability and the producer’s preference for value over volume.
Operational challenges and a shortage of immediate catalysts have also weighed on uranium shares, Argonaut deputy research head Jon Scholtz wrote in an Oct. 12 update . Contracting remains below replacement levels even as the longer-term supply outlook tightens, he wrote.
Company setbacks
Cameco (TSX: CCO; NYSE: CCJ) illustrates the operating pressures. The company reported third-quarter adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization of C$267 million ($191 million), 44% below BMO Capital Markets’ forecast, mining analyst Alexander Pearce wrote on Friday.
Lower uranium sales and higher unit costs drove much of the shortfall. Attributable production of 3.5 million lb. missed BMO’s forecast by 19%, while sales of 5.6 million lb. were 18% below expectations. The realized uranium price of $65.80 per lb. met expectations, Pearce wrote.
Cameco narrowed its annual production forecast to 19.5 million–20.5 million lb., from 19.5 million–21.5 million, and raised uranium cost-of-sales guidance to C$67–70 per lb., from C$63–67.50, in its results on Friday .
The Key Lake maintenance shutdown extended into the fourth quarter, leaving a risk to production if the restart is delayed, Desjardins mining analyst Bryce Adams wrote on Friday.
Increased engagement with customers reassessing fuel availability and supply security could support near-term contracting, Adams wrote. He maintained his buy recommendation and C$190 target.
Cameco shares eased 0.5% to C$116.63 in Toronto on Thursday, ahead of Friday’s results, valuing the company at about C$50.8 billion. The stock has traded between C$107.55 and C$182.72 over the past year.
Years to production
At NexGen Energy’s (TSX: NXE; NYSE: NXE) Rook I project in Saskatchewan, construction began in June, with first ore targeted for the third quarter of 2030, according to its October presentation .
Early work appeared consistent with management’s assessment that construction was on schedule and budget, Red Cloud Securities research head David Talbot wrote after an Oct. 22 site visit.
Ground freezing in early 2027 and shaft sinking into basement rock in 2028 remain important tests. Talbot expected prepayments or project debt, or a combination of the two, to cover about C$1.2 billion of remaining funding needs in late 2026 or early 2027.
NexGen shares fell 3.6% to C$12.06 in Toronto on Thursday, leaving them about 36% below their 52-week high of C$18.91.
Existing infrastructure also takes time to return to service. Anfield Energy (TSXV: AEC; NASDAQ: AEC) received draft licensing and groundwater permitting documents for its Shootaring Canyon mill in Utah on Oct. 21, the company said in an update on Tuesday .
Anfield targets licence renewal in the second quarter of 2027. That timetable, followed by about a year of construction, points towards production around mid-2028, Talbot wrote on Oct. 28. Financing for about $117 million of initial capital also remains necessary, he wrote.
Anfield shares weakened 1.4% to C$4.37 on the TSX Venture Exchange on Thursday.
Calmer financial markets, additional utility contracts and progress on production, permits and financing could help reconnect uranium shares with fuel-market conditions, Wong argued.
“The current divergence can persist longer than fundamental investors expect,” he wrote. “Liquidity regimes turn on the market’s timetable.”

In our transportation reporting, we rarely come across something as fun as today’s review of the Jasion Poki.
The Poki is a severely overpowered electric minibike that looks like it came from yesteryear. If the power isn’t enough, it also packs some cool tricks, and we’re not (just) talking about wheelies this time.
Jasion Poki by the numbers:
6,720W: Massive peak power from its central mid-drive motor. There’s a 2kW label on our early review model, which we reviewed thinking something was up. Turns out we were right; this is a powerhouse.
260 N·m: Raw, low-end torque to launch the bike forward. And Wheelies!
60V 30Ah: The hefty lithium-ion battery capacity built into the base chassis. Under the seat with a relatively high center of gravity..
50 mph: Jasion’s top speed. As a 200lber, I acheived 44mph crouched on flat ground. It shouldn’t even go this fast. I don’t think it would hit 50 without a 90-pounder wearing lycra behind the handlebars.
60 miles of range : At 30-40mph, expect closer to half that range
137.5 lbs: The substantial net weight of the bike, making it a heavy lift for manual transport.
So taking a look at this bad boy, it just screams fun. It is really low to the ground, has a big, wide seat large enough for 2 people as long as they are under 350lbs total, and has pegs for 2 people and a basket, great for carrying a picnic and an extra helmet.
Heavy duty
This thing is built like a tank, and it tips the scales accordingly. Getting this thing in my SUV ruptured a few discs in my back, though its compact nature means it fit quite well. Loosen the handlebars and it is downright compact. But that weight is strangely like 50lbs heavier than I would expect at close to 140lbs.
Advertisement - scroll for more content
That also makes the built-in wheelies a little bit more suspect. My son, who is by now becoming an expert at wheelies, found this one to be a bit more difficult than the auto wheelies on bikes like the Anyland or new Yozma IN11.
The fun part
OK so not only does this little powerhouse get you (and your friend) around town in style and it also makes wheelies a bit easier; but it also has a huge Bluetooth speaker in the back that sounds like a Harley and is all synced up with the actual controller so it sounds real.
Sure, it is a gimmick, but it is a fun one, and it might actually make the low-down bike a little safer since it is going to be out of the sight of most cars.
Electrek’s take:
I love this thing. It is my favorite bike to go to the beach on (and it does well in the sand with those fat tires). But I think there are some big misses here. First of all, it has no business going over 40mph. Not only does it feel scary with those tiny wheels, but speed wobbles puts both the rider a possible second rider at significant risk here. This is a fun bike and it should top out at 20-28mph max. Keep all the torque, just cut out the power at a reasonable top speed.
Also it should weigh a lot less. At 140lbs, it is silly hard to get into the back of a car, which it easily fits in. Making the frame aluminum would go a long way here. Also, if this thing rolled on top of you, it would be a bad day.
Make this thing safer and more portable, and I’d recommend everyone with a beach commute to get one. As it stands, best for responsible adults with strong backs and a Peter Pan complex.

Regeneron executives struck an upbeat tone on an investor call Friday as the biotech posted a consensus-beating $5.1 billion in third quarter earnings and CEO Leonard Schleifer touted the company’s ‘disease agnostic’ pipeline and approach to business development.
Regeneron executives touted “record sales” for some of the big biotech’s key products, striking a tone of ascension as the company opened trading on Friday morning up more than 11% to around $913 per share.
RBC Capital Markets called the third quarter a “clean sweep” for Regeneron, with revenue of $5.1 billion coming in “well above” the expected $4.61–$4.65 billion. The haul was a 36% increase over Q3 2025, according to Regeneron’s press release .
Meanwhile, BMO Capital Markets called Q3 a “clean quarter” for Regeneron, with “beats across the board highlight improving commercial outlook.”
CEO Leonard Schleifer in a statement attributed the strong showing to “record net sales,” for Sanofi-partnered inflammatory blockbuster Dupixent as well as the high-dose eye medicine Eylea HD and cancer immunotherapy Libtayo.
Earnings
Regeneron’s ‘aversion’ to M&A questioned as bumper Q2 builds war chest
Calls for Regeneron to step up dealmaking have intensified as the company has established an $18 billion cash pile and suffered clinical trial setbacks.

Dupixent continued to be a superstar for Regeneron and partner Sanofi, recording a 35% year-over-year increase with $6.5 billion in global sales—the first time the biologic had cleared the $5 billion mark, Schleifer said on a Friday morning investor call. Meanwhile, U.S. sales of Eylea HD leapt 62% to $699 million and Libtayo more than doubled year-over-year to $550 million.
Looking forward, Regeneron highlighted key upcoming catalysts for what Schleifer dubbed the biotech’s “disease agnostic” R&D pipeline.
First up, Regeneron is anticipating an FDA decision for cemdisiran, a subcutaneous siRNA therapy targeting C5, in November. If approved, cemdisiran would be the first siRNA therapy for myasthenia gravis, Regeneron Chief Scientific Officer George Yancopoulos said on the call. It would also be the only treatment to offer quarterly subcutaneous dosing, Schleifer added.
A former neurologist who cared for “many patients” with myasthenia gravis, Schleifer said it is “particularly gratifying” to see his company bring forward a potential new treatment option in this space.
Schleifer and Yancopoulos also highlighted a recent presentation at the European Society for Medical Oncology (ESMO) meeting of four-year follow-up data from the Phase 3 C-POST trial studying Libtayo as an adjuvant treatment for patients with high-risk cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma. The PD-1 inhibitor showed a 37% reduction in the risk of death at a median of 44 months, up from 22% at a median follow up of 30 months, the company reported on Monday.
Libtayo was approved by the FDA in October 2025 as the first and only immunotherapy for this indication.
On the obesity front, Yancopoulos pointed to Phase 3 data from olatorepatide, the dual GLP-1/GIP receptor agonist that Regeneron licensed in June 2025 from the Chinese biopharma Hansoh Pharmaceuticals for close to $2 billion in biobucks. In the China-based Phase 3 trial, olatorepatide elicited an up to 19% reduction in body weight at 48 weeks, according to a March 9 press release. At the time, Regeneron planned to launch a global Phase 3 trial for the drug this year.
Immunology and inflammation
Sanofi pays Regeneron $1B upfront to continue search for Dupixent successor
Sanofi and Regeneron have had a long and “sometimes contentious” partnership, BMO Capital Markets noted, as the companies contend with the looming loss of exclusivity of their blockbuster drug Dupixent.

Addressing a question on Regeneron’s potential place in the obesity race, Yancopoulos said the company’s objective is “not to just compete commercially with the Me Too but to give our commercial group an agent that really makes a difference for patients,” citing the need for an option that can address the challenge of muscle loss seen with other drugs in the class.
The executives also touched on Regeneron’s recently updated partnership with Sanofi in which the French pharma fronted $1 billion to advance four long-acting, next-generation antibodies for immune-mediated conditions. Beyond the sizeable upfront payment, the new deal could bring in up to $7 billion more for Regeneron in development, regulatory and commercial milestones.
The renewal was seen as somewhat of a détente for what BMO Capital Markets on Oct. 1 called the “sometimes contentious” partnership. Just last year, Regeneron sued Sanofi, alleging that the French pharma did not provide “full access to material information” about Dupixent’s sales.
“We have a very good relationship right now with Sanofi. I think we’re back on a very strong track,” Schleifer said in response to an analyst question on the new collaboration.
New Sanofi CEO Belén Garijo “has been really clear cut in helping us frame that we want to continue to build on Dupixent for a long time,” Schleifer added. Garijo took the reins at Sanofi in April after former CEO Paul Hudson was let go two months earlier.
“This was an exceptional quarter by every measure,” Schleifer said. “Our three core growth brands are performing at record levels, and our expanded alliance with Sanofi positions us to lead the next era of type 2 inflammation medicines.”
In response to a question from TD Cowen analyst Tyler Van Buren on whether Regeneron would become “even more aggressive on the business development front than it was a year ago,” Schleifer said the company is “open to any and all opportunities at all stages.
“We love platforms if we can get platforms, but we have the firepower to do an advanced product or an early stage,” he said. “So we are sort of agnostic.”

By Charlotte Goldstone
30 October 2026
Congestion today could mean a fresh wave of disputed detention and demurrage (D&D) charges tomorrow, according to Sara Dandan, founder of FourOneOne.
She told The Loadstar disruption at ports, including growing backlogs of containers at Los Angeles and Long Beach, was likely to translate into extra invoices in the coming weeks.
“Today’s problem is actually tomorrow’s problem,” said Ms Dandan. “If there is congestion in October, those invoices usually start hitting in November.”
She pointed to reports of 34,000 containers waiting for rail at Los Angeles and Long Beach, alongside growing difficulties returning empty containers, as terminals struggle to clear backlogs. Looming port strikes are also expected to exacerbate these issues.
Such circumstances could leave truckers exposed to charges, despite the delays being outside their control, added Ms Dandan.
However, the US Federal Maritime Commission (FMC) has established that the purpose of demurrage and detention fees is to incentivise the movement of cargo, rather than penalise operators for circumstances they cannot influence.
Where delays result from terminal closures, unavailable appointments, holidays, or restrictions on empty container returns, Ms Dandan argued, the rationale for imposing charges should no longer apply.
“It’s much more often that you can’t return it [a box], or you can’t pick it up, than it is that you just didn’t,” she said.
Nevertheless, Ms Dandan noted that many operators paid invoices rather than dispute them, either to avoid delaying operations or because challenging relatively small amounts can be prohibitively expensive.
For smaller drayage businesses, even small bills can threaten their survival, while the cost of hiring lawyers or dedicating staff to lengthy complaints processes often makes fighting individual invoices uneconomical.
“It’s death by a thousand invoices,” Ms Dandan said.
She has designed Provar, which approaches its first anniversary in December, a platform to address that imbalance by collecting and preserving the evidence needed to challenge improper charges.
It documents terminal conditions, appointment availability, and empty-return restrictions, preserving evidence to establish whether operators had a reasonable opportunity to collect or return containers during periods in question.
Provar covers terminals in Los Angeles, Long Beach, Oakland, and Seattle. Users submit their active containers, allowing the platform to automatically identify the relevant terminal and compile the supporting evidence.
A dispute function helps users easily prepare formal fee challenges by combining invoices, dispute reasons, and supporting documentation into a downloadable PDF letter for submission to the shipping line.
The platform also incorporates digital integrity verification to help establish that the underlying evidence has not been altered, addressing concerns about the reliability of evidence submitted in disputes.
Ms Dandan said the aim was to make challenging charges viable for businesses of every size, rather than leaving operators to absorb costs because the administrative burden outweighed the invoice.
“Whether you’re a humongous trucker with thousands of containers, or whether you only have a dozen, it’s still the same principle,” she said. “It empowers them to do more and do it more effectively.”
However, she warned that shipping lines’ evidentiary requirements were becoming “increasingly demanding”, with some requiring documentation of empty-return restrictions extending beyond the date of the disputed charge.
FourOneOne has introduced a ‘plus one’ feature to document those conditions in advance.
Ultimately, Ms Dandan believes that making disputes quicker, cheaper, and better supported by objective evidence could also change behaviour among shipping lines.

Schneider National announced Thursday it has inked a deal to utilize Norfolk Southern’s rail network in the East. The announcement was in conjunction with the multimodal transportation provider’s third-quarter report, which was slightly worse than expected.
New Norfolk Southern service agreement
Schneider said its new service agreement with Norfolk Southern ( NYSE: NSC ) will make the company the only entirely asset-based provider on a single-line transcontinental railroad in the U.S., assuming the railroad’s merger with peer Union Pacific ( NYSE: UNP ) is approved. (Schneider transferred its Western intermodal business to Union Pacific in 2023.)
Schneider’s intermodal service is executed with its own drivers and tractors, chassis (23,900), containers (26,800) and over 60 rail hubs in North America.
“As we transition our primary eastern rail provider to Norfolk Southern, we’ll expand access to key markets, increase network flexibility and create new opportunities to better serve our customers,” said Michael Baumgardt, executive vice president of intermodal and logistics at Schneider. “It will strengthen Schneider’s competitive position and enhance the reliable service experience our customers expect.”
The new service begins in January.
Schneider pointed to the success it has had with CPKC’s ( NYSE: CP ) cross-border, steel-wheel service as a factor in its decision to switch providers. Schneider said the move doesn’t jeopardize its existing relationship with CPKC. Schneider was an early user of the Southeast Mexico Express (SMX), a joint offering from CSX ( NASDAQ: CSX ) and CPKC, connecting Mexico to Texas and to the Southeast U.S.
“I mean, if you look at the UP today, we’re using the CPKC out of Mexico, despite the fact that they have a service,” said Jim Filter, Schneider president and CEO, on a call with analysts. “And they continue to operate with us and love everything that we’re doing with them, but they understand there’s a place that we don’t use them. And so, it’s not that unusual that you’re not going to go with one provider for everything.”
SONAR: Intermodal Contract Savings Index (IMCSI.USA). The IMCSI shows the savings percentage between domestic intermodal contract rate per mile and truckload contract rate per mile. The comparison includes fuel surcharges. To learn more about SONAR, click here .
Noisy Q3 on path to recovery
Schneider ( NYSE: SNDR ) reported adjusted earnings per share of 29 cents for the third quarter, a penny below consensus but 17 cents higher year over year. Net interest expense was a 5-cent y/y tailwind, in part due to a reversal of interest accruals tied to a claim settlement (3 cents). A lower tax rate also helped slightly. But a separate claim in its logistics segment partially offset these benefits.
Consolidated revenue of $1.59 billion was 9% higher y/y and slightly better than the $1.58-billion consensus estimate.
It raised the bottom end of its full-year adjusted EPS guidance range by 10 cents to a new range of $1 to $1.10. The consensus estimate was $1.06 at the time of the print. (The company reported full-year 2025 adjusted EPS of 63 cents.)
Table: Schneider’s key performance indicators
Truckload revenue (ex-fuel) was flat y/y at $625 million as an 8% increase in revenue per truck (ex-fuel) was offset by an 8% decline in average trucks in service. The utilization metric was 3% higher y/y for its dedicated fleet and 21% higher for the one-way fleet.
One-way contract renewals averaged just under 20% in the quarter, as management said that the capacity crackdown is expanding . This allowed the fleet to return to profitability.
The company has sold dedicated service on 850 trucks this year, but is still working to offset a previously disclosed customer loss.
The TL unit reported a 93% operating ratio (inverse of operating margin ), which was 380 basis points better y/y, but 120 bps worse than the second quarter .
Intermodal revenue (ex-fuel) increased 2% y/y to $288 million. A 2% decline in loads was offset by a 3% increase in revenue per load (ex-fuel). Intermodal contract renewals are “comfortably in the mid-single-digit range,” management said. The unit reported a 92.1% OR, 190 bps better y/y.
The logistics segment reported breakeven results as a confidential claim settlement negatively impacted the period.
Net debt leverage was 0.1x at the end of the quarter, down from 0.3x at the end of 2025. Schneider lowered its full-year net capex plan to a range of $325 million to $350 million. Net capex totaled $289 million in 2025.
Why it matters? Schneider’s new service agreement with Norfolk Southern expands its market access and potentially establishes it as a unique asset-based provider on a single-line transcontinental rail network alongside its growing cross-border intermodal service. Meanwhile, Schneider’s results serve as a bellwether for the health of the truckload and intermodal markets.

Couple Spent $1 Million on an Endless Cruise, Were Kicked Off It After 2 Years
19 photos
Photo: Randy Cassingham with permission from ResidentialCruising.com
There's no use in crying over spilled milk, but the urge to do so must feel irresistible when you sold your home and all your land-bound possessions in order to afford the milk that someone else spilled for you. Or, in this case, the cruise ship that should have kept circumnavigating the world non-stop ever 3.5 years.
Earlier this month, Villa Vie Residences (VVR), a Florida-based startup that promised never-ending cruises that would change the way people lived "globally" at sea, announced that their flagship Odyssey would cease operations immediately . The result was 203 guests and 156 crew getting kicked off the ship and left stranded in a port in Cambodia, with the exception of a skeleton crew that would continue on for maintenance.
As of the Odyssey, it would remain laid up until management could find a solution out of the predicament, whether that be a new investor and cash infusion or file for bankruptcy. The guests were given less than six hours to gather all their belongings and disembark, without as much as being offered some guidance regarding local accommodation, at least at first.
For them, the Odyssey wasn't yet another cruise ship, small as it might be. This was their home or the place they hopped to call that for at least the next 15 years, because that's what VVR had promised them.
Photo: Villa Vie Residences That's what this novel way of living at sea entailed: full ownership of a cabin on a ship that would circumnavigate the globe continuously every 3.5 years, before it would head in for regular maintenance and then depart again. VVR offered at-sea residences (villas), but they also sold more traditional cruises – the segments that made up that 3.5-year continuous cruise.
It was imagined as an all-encompassing solution for anyone for whom a cruise is the perfect way to spend the time. You could either dip a toe and get onboard as an occasional guest, joining the residents for cruises ranging from one week to a couple of months, or you could go all-in and buy a cabin – to live in or to rent.
Buying a cabin meant getting to enjoy a new lifestyle , one where you could combine the advantages of being a perpetual tourist/traveler to residential comfort. You could basically work from anywhere, while having all the house chores handled by someone else, with the bonus of having views that changed everyday.
Photo: Villa Vie Residences To boot, VVR promised all these things at prices that could still be called affordable. At the time the Odyssey was launched, VVR cited the high costs of living and the higher prices of other cruises as perfect examples of why this type of lifestyle could not fail.
You have to admit, the idea is appealing even today, when we know that the Odyssey pulled into port, kicked off all the guests, and was declared "over" despite promises that the dream would live on for at least 15 years after the 2024 departure.
Guests still in Cambodia, still waiting for some kind of clarification from the VVR management, are starting to talk to the media, offering a glimpse into their state of mind, their exact financial predicament, and their thoughts on how the adventure has ended. Among them is Randy Cassingham, who, with his wife Kit, was one of the full-time owners on the Odyssey .
Photo: Villa Vie Residences Cassingham is an American writer, humorist, and a pioneer in online publishing. His This Is True website was the first for-profit email letter, and he continues to be an active and well-regarded publisher of content. He was one of the first to embrace the Odyssey dream, buying a villa and moving onboard the second the ship was cleared for departure out of Belfast in 2024.
Some reports online claim that he was a Founder, so not a simple Resident, which would mean he'd invested in the VVR enterprise and, as such, had a stake in it. Cassingham never said so publicly, but he was always a supporter and cheerleader of the Odyssey dream.
He continues to be even now, when VVR has kicked him and his wife off the ship with everyone else. Speaking to the media out of Cambodia, he says they spent close to $1 million for what they believed would be their long-term, if not forever, home.
Photo: Villa Vie Residences This amount includes the $370,000 to $380,000 they initially paid for their cabin on the Odyssey and the $7,000 a month in expenses since they boarded. Every villa on the Odyssey came with a fixed price tag depending on its location and amenities (balcony, size, the usual on a cruise ship), but residents still had to pay variable amounts on a monthly basis for stuff like housekeeping, medical visits, food and drinks, and other options.
Cassingham says this two-year experience was "great, money aside," adding that it was "fantastic" that they could travel the world and have so many experience during this time. Neither he nor his wife has any regrets, even though they sold their home in the U.S. and even their car in order to get onboard.
It seems like the key to this kind of upbeat attitude in the face of financial disaster comes from the deliberate decision to get into the adventure knowing that it might fail at any moment. Cassingham has previously spoken about a "cascade of problems" that he and all residents had witnessed in 2026, including meeting with management to try and raise money from the residents to pay for fuel and cost-cutting measures like slower travels and longer stays in port.
Photo: Villa Vie Residences Cassignham doesn't expect any kind of refund from VVR, because he knows they've run out of money. He also knows that he doesn't really "own" anything on the Odyssey : despite the pompous-sounding terminology, VVR sold rights to occupy, not actual ownership.
Still, he insists, the past two years have been a dream of an adventure, and they were worth it.

Word on the street is that the next-gen Camaro could be offered as a four-door sedan strictly, presumably with V8 firepower, and maybe an optional stick shift. It remains to be seen whether this is true or not, but meanwhile, those who want a Chevy muscle car must search the used market for that perfect example.
And if the fifth generation gets your heart racing, then you have come to the right place, because you have the chance to buy the one pictured in the gallery. This machine has a single owner in the papers who bought it new in May 2012. The man paid $60,384 for the car, as per the attached window sticker, and has put 32,000 miles (51,500 km) on it.
Thus, it is not a high-mileage example, and the fact that it has a single owner in the papers definitely makes it more appealing. But there are some downsides, as this Chevrolet Camaro ZL1 has a check engine light on, some wear on the driver’s seat, chips on the front bumper, and scratches on the rear one. It was also involved in an accident in February 2019, sustaining “minor damage” to the rear end.
Photo: Cars&Bids Moreover, it also has extensive modifications . It features a 416-cubic-inch LSA V8 long block engine under the hood with a Kong Performance supercharger. It also has new ported and polished cylinder heads, a new camshaft, an LSA crankshaft, a new oil pump, and upper supercharger pulley, lower crank pulley, and throttle body that came from the aftermarket world.
Since we mentioned the engine, we might as well tell you that the 6.8-liter supercharged V8 has undisclosed output and thrust, and works in concert with a six-speed automatic transmission.
The new fuel injectors, auxiliary fuel pump system, dual fuel pump system, air intake, exhaust headers, exhaust system, and others have also come from the tuning world. Additional modifications include the exterior lights, front grille, illuminated door handles, black rear bowtie emblem, carbon fiber pattern hydro-dipped trim, and an AEM gauge on the inside.
Some of the factory equipment includes the Magnetic Ride Control suspension, Brembo brakes, limited-slip differential, and 20-inch forged aluminum wheels. This old Chevy Camaro ZL1 also has a head-up display, heated front seats, and a power sunroof, among others.
Photo: Cars&Bids The service history is said to be detailed in the Carfax history report. The muscle car has an Ashen Gray Metallic exterior, a black cabin, and a clean Florida title. It is located in Saint Augustine, FL, and accompanied by the factory door handles, grille, two blower covers, a trunk organizer, a car cover, a set of floor mats, a carbon fiber hood insert, the window sticker, and two keys.
Interested parties should know that this Chevrolet Camaro ZL1 may not pass emissions testing in some states due to the modifications. This machine has been indeed registered to one owner in New Mexico and Florida since new, the Carfax report shows, and there are no mileage discrepancies. The car has 2024 date codes on the tires, and tinted windows.
A 2012 Chevrolet Camaro ZL1 is valued at $30,000 to $45,000 in today’s used car market. Collector grade examples, with under 10,000 miles (16,000 km), can exceed $50,000. A good daily driver with 30,000 to 60,000 miles (48,000-96,000 km) on the odo is valued at over $30,000, and high-mileage machines in rough condition cost less than $30,000.
This one definitely looks good, and the fact that it has been registered to the same person since it left the dealership back in 2012 definitely adds to the hype. Due to the modifications , however, it may not be everyone’s cup of tea, so we are curious to see how much it fetches when the gavel hits the table, because it is currently advertised on Cars&Bids as part of an ongoing online auction that will end four days from now, next Tuesday, on November 3, 2026.
At the time of writing, this Chevy Camaro ZL1 had a high bid of $6,767. There is a reserve on it, and it has obviously not been met. The owner hasn’t revealed why he wants it gone, but to be honest, he has had it for the for more than 14 years, and that’s plenty of time to get bored with every ride out there, regardless of the make and model.
Care to buy this modified muscle car? In that case, you will have to bid on it and win the online auction that you can access here on the quoted website. That is also where you can check out this Chevy Camaro ZL1 in more detail. How much is something like this worth in your opinion?

By Gavin van Marle
30 October 2026
Container spot freight rates on the transpacific eastbound trade, as recorded by Drewry, saw its steepest one-week fall since June 2025 after this year’s protracted peak season came to an end.
Drewry’s World Container Index (WCI) saw the spot rate on its Shanghai-Los Angeles decline 6% week on week, to end at $7,514 per 40ft, while the Shanghai-New York route was down 5%, to $9,631 per 40ft.
“Strong US import demand is easing,” Drewry noted.
“According to the US National Retail Federation, US ocean import volumes are forecast to decrease 11% month on month in November, which could put further downward pressure on freight rates,” it added.
However, in a sign that the market is in a state of flux, US forwarders reported a “stable” week, rather than one characterised by falling prices.
“Pricing carried over from last week, while space availability improved and vessel schedules became more consistent,” explained US west coast forwarder Freight Right. “As the traditional pre-holiday ocean shipping peak fully closes out, pricing has settled into a steady holding pattern across both coasts.”
However, it added that, with demand weakening and the remaining urgent pre-holiday shipments now transferring to air freight, the chances of the new general rate increase (GRI), scheduled for Sunday (1 November) – ranging from $2,000 to $3,000 per 40ft depending on carrier – sticking, were diminishing.
“China-to-US ocean rates are expected to remain broadly stable through the first half of November, with the possibility of modest declines. Improving space availability and more consistent schedules suggest limited near-term upward pressure on pricing,” said Freight Right.
The WCI on the Asia-Europe was essentially flat this week, as the surprising spot rate strength in October continued.
The WCI’s Shanghai-Rotterdam leg was up 1%, to $3,686 per 40ft, while Shanghai-Genoa route was held steady, at $4,151 per 40ft, although this masked some discounting by carriers keen to fill ships amid weak demand, and despite new FAK (freight all kinds) levels due to be implemented on Sunday.
These will see MSC target a spot rate of $4,500 per 40ft on Asia-North Europe, $5,000 on Asia-west Mediterranean and $5,100 on Asia-east Mediterranean, while CMA CGM is aiming for $4,900 on Asia-west Mediterranean and $5,200 on Asia-east Mediterranean ports.
However, Linerlytica this week noted: “Asia-North Europe rates remain under pressure, with carriers undermining their 1 November rate hike efforts with persistent discounts.
“Gemini carriers are offering the lowest rates in the spot market for early November shipments, with Hapag-Lloyd at $3,000-$3,200 per 40ft and Maersk at $3,200-$3,400 per 40ft.
“Their rivals at MSC, the Ocean Alliance, and Premier Alliance have reacted by lowering their rate offers to $3,400 to $3,500 per 40ft. The 1 November rate hike is effectively doomed,” it added.
Meanwhile, with the Asia-Europe contract tendering season now in full swing, carriers are trying to push up spot rates that act as a guide for annual rate negotiations, and yesterday announced another set of FAK increases for 15 November, with MSC upping its Asia-North Europe spot rate to $4,600, and to $5,300 per 40ft on West Mediterranean destinations, and CMA CGM aiming for $5,500 per 40ft on Asia-west Med shipments.
According to Drewry’s Container Capacity Insight, four blanked sailings have been announced for next week, down from eight this week, as the analysts also doubted success for the new FAK levels.
“Given available capacity and weak demand, it remains uncertain whether these increases will hold. Hence, Drewry expects rates to remain stable next week,” it said.

Indian Turquoise 1957 Chrysler New Yorker With Old-School Hemi Is Pure Eye Candy
14 photos
Photo: volocars.com
Introduced in 1940 and produced through 1996, the New Yorker is Chrysler's longest-running nameplate . It's also one of the division's most iconic models. Much like the 300 letter series, the New Yorker is a desirable classic today.
As with all Mopars, I'm a big fan of the Forward Look-era New Yorker. Virgil Exner's now-iconic styling language debuted in 1955. The early design was based on his custom 1952 Imperial Parade Phaeton. The last Forward Look vehicles were produced in 1962.
The Forward Look Chryslers got their first major facelift in 1957. That's when the New Yorker gained quad headlamps and a grille that extended toward the front wheel arches. The tailfins also became significantly bigger. It's arguably my favorite of the bunch, and it's precisely why I'm showing you this 1957 drop top. This and the fact that it's an absolute gem.
The New Yorker was pretty popular for an expensive luxury car in 1957; Chrysler sold 34,620 units. However, two body styles stand out as rare. The Town & Country station wagon , for instance, was built in only 1,391 examples. The two-door convertible is even rarer, with only 1,049 units delivered. Significantly fewer of them are still around.
But rarity isn't the only thing this New Yorker can brag about. It's also one of those classics that's been restored to Concours-ready condition. The overhaul took a whopping 2,000 hours and resulted in an outstanding vehicle inside and out.
Of course, the Indian Turquoise paint and the massive amount of chrome help this land yacht stand out. The same goes for the two-tone, turquoise/white interior. This thing is pure eye candy, which isn't surprising given that the restoration cost a whopping $250,000.
If you're into shiny engine bays, this New Yorker delivers. If you ever wanted to see how a 1957 Chrysler mill looked when it rolled off the assembly line, this 392-cubic-inch (6.4-liter) V8 is exactly what you need. It's also an old-school Hemi, if you're into that.
Chrysler introduced its first Hemi engine, also known as FirePower, in 1951. Originally a 331-cubic-inch (5.4-liter) mill, the FirePower grew to 354 cubic inches (5.8 liters) in 1956. The following year, Chrysler debuted the 392-cubic-inch V8 you see here.
This engine was produced for only two model years. In addition to the New Yorker, it also powered the 300C, 300D, and the flagship Imperial line (Custom, Crown, and LeBaron). The powerplant delivered 325 horsepower in the New Yorker.

Focused on ensuring growth beyond Dupixent, Sanofi wants to acquire derisked assets that may benefit from the French pharma’s commercial capabilities, executives said on Friday as they reported third-quarter earnings.

The French drugmaker plans to use its “robust cash flow generation to fund business development and M&A transactions, in particular with a focus on later-stage and/or commercial opportunities,” Sanofi CEO Belén Garijo said on the company’s third-quarter earnings call. Sanofi CFO François Roger added that a “strong balance sheet and low leverage allow us to access external financing” to fund deals for the next set of growth drivers.
“We are laser-focused on ensuring growth beyond Dupixent [loss of exclusivity],” Garijo said. “We know that the pipeline and the R&D research will take a bit of time to materialize and bear fruits. Moving to later-stage commercial assets will allow us to derisk scientifically and clinically but also leverage our commercial capabilities much better.”
Garijo was speaking after a quarter in which Sanofi’s cornerstone drug Dupixent and struggling vaccine franchise outperformed expectations. Sanofi posted net sales of €14.4 billion ($16.1 billion), beating the €13.3 billion ($14.0 billion) consensus estimate that Guggenheim Securities analysts shared in a note to investors Friday. Sanofi’s net sales increased 14.3% at a constant exchange rate.
For the full year, Sanofi now expects sales to grow by a low-teens percentage at constant currencies. The company had forecast full-year growth of about 10% in July and was aiming to achieve high single-digit growth when it reported its first quarter results in April.
Dupixent sales increased 34.8%, climbing to almost €5.7 billion ($5.3 billion). Sanofi attributed the fast growth to strong demand across a range of indications. Guggenheim analysts expected Sanofi to report Dupixent sales of just under €5 billion ($5.6 billion).
Sanofi’s reliance on Dupixent, which accounted for 39% of net sales in the quarter, is a focus for analysts ahead of a 2031 patent expiry. Newer products are growing but remain small compared to Dupixent. Led by the hemophilia A drug Altuviiio, a set of 13 launch products generated €1.4 billion ($1.6 billion) in the quarter, up 31.4% from the same period last year.
Vaccine sales, meanwhile, fell 6.6%. Yet, at €3.2 billion ($3.6 billion), they still beat the €2.8 billion ($3.1 billion) forecast by Guggenheim analysts. Walmart has committed approximately $6 billion to expand its work with Symbotic, including additional automation at 25 U.S. regional distribution centers . The agreement covers spending over several years across multiple locations.
What’s Related
The companies said the work will help Walmart store more inventory and improve how products move through its distribution centers. Walmart expects the changes to help it offer a wider selection and replenish inventory more reliably.
The spending covers purchases of Symbotic systems and funding for technology development. According to Symbotic's securities filing, it is an additional commitment separate from purchases Walmart has already agreed to under earlier contracts.
The agreement also provides for work in selected international markets in the Americas. The announcement did not identify the 25 U.S. distribution centers or give a completion date for the upgrades.

Rob Montgomery, executive vice president for Walmart U.S. Supply Chain Operations, said: “At Walmart, we're focused on bringing more items to more customers and members, faster than ever.”
Symbotic’s products include BreakPack, which picks individual items, and SymMicro, a small-scale fulfillment system for online orders. Its software uses AI to coordinate case movement through warehouses .

The commitment includes $125 million for research and development of new storage racks and related technology for picking, product movement, and inventory management. That amount is part of the approximately $6 billion total, according to the filing.
Walmart will also pay fees for each system it purchases, including software licenses, maintenance, spare parts, and support. Those fees are in addition to the initial commitment.

source_document.body:
By Alex Lennane
30 October 2026
The weather was dreadful, the blueberries were under suspicion, and there were people dressed as rats outside the convention centre. Inside, however, air cargo was in a remarkably good mood.
At TIACA’s Air Cargo Forum in Miami this week, the airlines had turned up in force, people wanted to do business, and anyone with a freighter on the transpacific had particular reason to enjoy themselves. (Although there may be less enjoyment from anyone trying to book space on it.)
One word that was heard surprisingly little was “peak”. The conversations were about strong demand from the AI sector continuing well beyond the point at which the industry traditionally takes down the decorations and starts worrying again. Various forecasts put next year’s demand growth at 5% or more; expectations for capacity growth were more mixed. But, having covered this industry for over a decade, I’ve never heard so many airlines crying-out for freighter capacity, normally a risky business. Conversions have shot up in price; and the delivery dates stretching out over the next several years may perhaps come too late for this current rush.
Adding to the uncertainty were rumours in Miami that Boeing might not make use of its FAA exemption to keep delivering the current 777 freighter beyond 2027. Unconfirmed, but hardly comforting for anyone hoping the aircraft shortage might resolve itself.
The broader concern in Miami was capacity: where to find it; how to secure it; and how long the squeeze might last.
Even ecommerce, whose demise has been so eagerly discussed, was still taking up space. Down on some lanes, yes. Out of the picture, certainly not. The parcels have declined to take the hint.
For shippers, a prolonged squeeze makes the relationship with their forwarders rather more consequential. Their message in Miami was straightforward: help us when things go wrong, and we will remember when it is time to award the next contract.
One shipper described rewarding a forwarder that had worked to protect agreed rates during a capacity crunch, rather than simply joining the queue with a surcharge. Others wanted practical alternatives when disruption struck. Loyalty still has commercial value, even if it is difficult to put in a procurement spreadsheet.
There was less enthusiasm for ‘yet another’ dashboard. A beautifully displayed problem remains a problem, although perhaps it is reassuring to know precisely which shade of amber your shipment has become.
Forwarders, meanwhile, had their own disappointments. One said he had emerged from a string of airline meetings finding the offerings distinctly “meh”. Little innovation; not much to get excited about.
With space in short supply, perhaps an airline can get away with a sales pitch that largely amounts solely to ‘having some’. But a market in which customers need you is also a useful opportunity to give them a reason to stay when they don’t.
Outside the venue, another industry relationship was receiving rather more theatrical scrutiny.
Union protesters dressed as rats were highlighting safety allegations against Alliance Ground International. Inside, AGI occupied a large stand at the main entrance to the exhibition hall. An awkward arrangement for anyone hoping visitors would encounter only the approved brand messaging.
AGI weathering the storm
Elsewhere, the mood was more affectionate, if occasionally tearful. Air cargo was saying goodbye to several familiar faces, and TIACA outgoing DG Glyn Hughes appeared determined to provide enough emotion for the entire departing cohort.
TIACA’s board had given him a send-off the night before the event started; a public ‘roast’ supplied further opportunities for him to reach for a tissue. Having spent years making sure there were no incriminating photographs of him, he had apparently failed to anticipate AI. A lifetime of photographic discipline, undone by a prompt.
With Mammen Tharakan taking over as DG, and Mr Hughes continuing part-time until January, the latter plans to spend some time ‘doing life’, before deciding what comes next. There are, unsurprisingly, plenty of invitations. The challenge may be persuading an industry accustomed to his availability that retirement is not simply a more flexible booking system.
TIACA’s Glyn Hughes, Roos Bakker and Mammen Tharakan
With new chair Roos Bakker too, a new era at TIACA is taking shape; younger, driven, and motivated. It’ll be great to watch to see how it thrives. Those problems stalking TIACA in the past, largely financial, seem to be now in the rear-view mirror. Long may that last.
And there were retirements elsewhere. A United Cargo party to say goodbye to cargo chief Jan Krems added to the sense of a generation handing over.
The US Airforwarders Association has also changed its guard. After 21 years of Brandon Fried, Steve Smith, previously chief executive of Airlink, has taken over. Affable and seemingly well suited to the job, he looks a good choice for a role requiring relationships, persistence, and the ability to both listen and explain.
Encouragingly, the farewells were accompanied by some arrivals. More than 100 students attended TIACA’s event, with a raffle among the proceedings. The industry spends a good deal of time discussing the next generation; it was nice to see them in the room.
And there were airlines. Plenty of them.
At the previous Miami event, finding a carrier in the exhibition hall was a surprisingly tough ask. This time, the Americas were particularly well represented in the hall, and a record 100 airlines were represented among the delegates, according to the organisers. Cathay took the crown for best stand – centrally located, with the best coffee (and the worst queues) and also serving carajillos – espresso fortified with liqueur, very efficiently combining the two principal fuels of any air cargo event.
Ever busy: Cathay Cargo’s stand
Attendance was put at around 3,000, although the hall did not always feel that busy. There were fewer stands than last time, but the mix felt better. The morning-only conference programme also worked well, leaving afternoons free for meetings.
Forwarders, as ever, were largely in those meetings, making them both reassuringly busy and extremely difficult to find.
For all the competition between air cargo events, there remains a pleasure in going to a key global one, and seeing people who, over the years, have become actual friends. New faces noted how welcoming everyone was, how readily people made introductions and helped them connect. It’s a considerable part of this industry’s appeal. People may be ferocious over a rate negotiation, but they will still introduce you to someone useful afterwards.
Miami itself – very much dressed for Halloween – was facing its own battles, with the weather. Horizontal rain and lashings of wind threatened the yoga, pickleball, and golf events – but, true to the industry, the disruption did not stop play. The weather also seemed to herald a metaphorical view ahead of next week’s US midterm elections. There were plenty of gloomy predictions about what may happen in the country next week – yet another possiiblity of a ‘black swan’ that people now expect to see more often than white swans.
Miami all dressed up
But inside the hall, people were motivated. There was freight to move, business to win, and a reasonable expectation that demand would keep them occupied well beyond the usual seasonal rush. The question was, how to carry it all.
And, it being Miami, there was also extensive discussion of perishables throughout the hall, including one earnestly confidential briefing on the alleged shortcomings of Peruvian blueberries.
I shall protect my source. Some relationships are too important to jeopardise over soft fruit.

source_document.body:
Honeywell Aerospace plans to build a $500 million manufacturing facility in Tempe, Arizona, adding production space and bringing more complex machining work in-house as suppliers struggle to keep up with demand.
What’s Related
The 300,000-square-foot factory will expand the company’s existing Tempe campus and is expected to open in late 2028. Honeywell said it will create about 600 permanent jobs over time, with construction adding more than 1,000 local jobs.
The plant will serve commercial aviation and defense customers, including production tied to $15 billion in new program wins for its Control Systems unit. It will also add capacity for defense technologies covered by a supplier agreement signed with the U.S. Department of War in March.
“Demand for technology from Honeywell Aerospace continues to accelerate across both commercial and defense markets, and this major investment ensures we can continue delivering for our customers while unlocking long-term growth for our shareholders,” said Jim Currier, president and CEO of Honeywell Aerospace.
Cutting need for outside suppliers
Some of Honeywell’s suppliers can’t produce enough of the precisely machined parts the company needs. The new plant will allow Honeywell to make more of those parts itself, reducing its reliance on outside suppliers.
The factory will also add production space for aircraft systems that customers have already ordered, including Honeywell’s Assure actuation systems and Attune cooling systems. Chief Financial Officer Josh Jepsen said those orders helped drive the decision to build the plant.
“It gives us more capacity. It gives us the ability to be more vertically integrated, control our own destiny a bit more,” Jepsen said on the company’s third-quarter earnings call.
Built around automation
The Tempe facility will combine modular robotics with automated inspection and digital twins . Honeywell also plans to use AI to help improve production and link manufacturing information through a connected digital system.
Honeywell said the plant will serve as a model for its future factories. It is intended to handle business already awarded while providing room to pursue additional aircraft programs.
Supplier shortages remain a problem
The expansion is part of a larger effort to address supply bottlenecks. In its third-quarter presentation, Honeywell said it had committed to bringing production of about 700 parts in-house, representing $100 million in annual spending. Honeywell didn’t say how much of that work will move to Tempe.
Honeywell’s backlog reached $19.3 billion at the end of the quarter, up 12% from a year earlier. Its earnings release said constraints at a small number of mechanical suppliers were limiting output growth.

“You don’t spend one and a half billion dollars without creating jobs,” AstraZeneca CEO Pascal Soriot said as the pharma announced a new cost savings program alongside third quarter earnings.
AstraZeneca has rolled out a $1.5 billion three-year cost savings program to redeploy resources to areas for growth. While no layoffs are expected, executives said the program will impact all areas of the business and could involve shifting certain workers and resources to support emerging areas.
“You don’t spend one and a half billion dollars without creating jobs,” CEO Pascal Soriot said on a Friday morning third quarter earnings call with media. “It’s more reallocation of resources across the pipeline and across the world. But in the end we are still a growing company, and the idea is not to shrink the company. The opposite, actually.”
The program has been dubbed the Reshaping for Sustainable Growth (RSG) program, with CFO Aradhana Sarin suggesting that “reshaping” is key to understanding the effort. The initial cost will be $2 billion, with a projected $1.5 billion in savings. AstraZeneca will work to “upskill” or “reskill” certain employees, hire new people or employ technology for efficiencies.
“The intention is to create capacity in the organization to absorb the growth that we’re expected to have without necessarily, you know, growing all through headcount,” Sarin said.
AstraZeneca booked $16.2 billion in total revenue for the quarter, a 7% jump over the same period a year before and 8% above consensus, Leerink Partners said in a Friday morning note. This total includes $15.1 billion in total product sales and $1.1 billion in alliance revenue. Oncology products delivered $7.1 billion—15% above Q3 2025—while rare disease grew 10% to $2.63 billion.
Oncology blockbuster Tagrisso had a particularly strong quarter, with worldwide sales of $2.2 billion for a 4% beat on consensus. The product is serving as the backbone treatment option for all stages of EGFR lung cancer, Leerink noted.
The strategy that AstraZeneca has deployed to build out Tagrisso will come into play in the pharma’s recent equity and clinical deals with Summit Therapeutics , Soriot said. The partners will work on different antibody-drug conjugate (ADC) combinations for cancer with the biotech’s China-developed PD-1/VEGF bispecific antibody ivonescimab.
“If we want to maximize the value of this ADC platform and bring physicians options that meet their needs, we need to combine with a PD-1/VEGF,” Soriot said.

Similarly, AstraZeneca has worked to test a combination of Tagrisso with two other agents for lung cancer to provide additional treatment options.
Soriot also suggested that the company is looking at potential business development activities in oncology, cardiovascular, rare disease, immunology and respiratory disease.
“We have a strong pipeline as it is.” Soriot said. “We can grow nicely beyond 2030, but we are constantly looking at how do we strengthen our presence in [one] franchise or another, in [one] disease or another, and how do we add more value to our portfolio in the company?”
AstraZeneca is also looking to China, despite recent efforts by the U.S. government to restrict collaborations. While the new policy from the U.S. Department of the Treasury are not yet set in stone, Soriot expressed support for keeping the lines of collaboration open.
“When they come up with new medicines that can help cancer patients, people will want it,” the CEO said. “You don’t really mind where it’s coming from originally.”
Soriot added that when AstraZeneca, a global company, picks up an asset from China, it is ultimately developed, commercialized and even manufactured in the U.S.
“For all intents and purposes, it becomes a U.S. product, saving U.S. lives,” Soriot said. “We stay alert of all these potential legal changes, and we will of course respect them. But it’s important to remember that in science, collaboration is important, and in cancer or other diseases, people will want access to medicines that can save their lives.”

VIENNA — German tank maker KNDS and Norway’s Ritek have begun producing Leopard 2A8 tanks in Norway, adding a land-based industrial foothold to a security partnership spanning submarines, missiles and military operations in Europe’s north.
Production started Oct. 15 in Levanger, where the companies will build 37 of the Norwegian Army’s 54 new tanks, KNDS said in an email. The facility took 18 months to establish and has a stated capacity of up to 36 tanks annually.
The production launch follows the partners’ inauguration of the manufacturing and testing infrastructure in late April. October’s milestone caps an existing procurement arrangement rather than marking a new tank purchase.
The industrial tie-up forms part of a broader mutual embrace that the two governments formalized in February through the sweeping Hansa Arrangement. Its priorities include maritime operations, combined-arms land warfare, rapid reinforcement, defense industry, and space-based surveillance, targeting and communications, according to a readout by Norway’s Defense Ministry.
An ongoing submarine partnership offers the clearest example of how equipment purchases can bind the countries’ armed forces and security strategies together. Both plan to operate six identical Type 212CD submarines, supported by cooperation on personnel training and new maintenance facilities at Haakonsvern, near Bergen, the Norwegian ministry said. Berlin and Oslo are also collaborating on the next-generation 3SM maritime strike missile.
Although industry cooperation forms the bedrock, the relationship is moving beyond mere procurement questions. Germany contributed approximately 1,800 troops to Norway’s Cold Response exercise in March, according to the German government. Norway said in February that discussions were underway about German equipment pre-positioning on its territory.
Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in early 2022 accelerated a longstanding partnership, researchers at the Norwegian Institute of International Affairs concluded in a December 2024 assessment. Germany’s growing dependence on Norwegian gas also strengthened its interest in protecting offshore infrastructure, researcher Øyvind Svendsen explained .
Germany’s military is undergoing a distinct shift toward a bigger role in the North Atlantic. Its new P-8A Poseidon aircraft, for example, are covering the so-called GIUK gap between Greenland, Iceland and the UK, a crucial area that Russian nuclear submarines must pass through to reach the open Atlantic. German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius said the aircraft would operate from Norwegian and Icelandic air bases for this mission, Defense News previously reported .
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and Jonas Gahr Støre, Prime Minister of Norway, sit next to each other at the Andøya Space Visitor Center during the “Round Table on Space Cooperation” in Andenes, Norway, on Feb. 20, 2026. (Soeren Stache/picture alliance via Getty Images)
Space cooperation offers another avenue for growing collaboration. During a March visit to Andøya, Pistorius identified a joint imaging-reconnaissance satellite constellation as a project he wanted to pursue, according to his ministry.
In April, Oslo and Berlin agreed to create a bilateral space working group, with priorities including launch capabilities, space-based surveillance and secure communications. Norway is home to a valuable spaceport on the island of Andøya, which is particularly well situated for launching satellites into polar orbits, which are preferable for spy satellites.
The two North Sea countries are also cooperating in a number of other formats, including under the Multinational Multi Role Tanker Transport Fleet, which pools access to Airbus A330 MRTT aircraft for aerial refueling, strategic transport and medical evacuation, and EU HYDEF, where Germany and Norway are among five co-funders working on phase one of a European hypersonic interceptor missile.
